item.title: Jordan inherits House GOP fight over punishing rebels
item.description:
One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership.

Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership.

  • The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios.

Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes, a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic.

  • Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision.
  • Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings.
  • Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals.

The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress.

  • One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference.
  • Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes.
  • "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal.

Zoom in: House Republicans have long discussed the concept, and there's support across the conference, including from incoming Minority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), who advocated for consequences in an interview with Axios on the campaign trail in October.

  • A GOP lawmaker told Axios that support extends beyond Main Street, with members in the Republican Study Committee pushing similar proposals.

The intrigue: Jordan comes from a wing of the party known for challenging GOP leaders, who employ the very tactics Main Street Republicans are now seeking to rein in.

  • But Main Street Republicans represent a significant bloc of the conference, giving Jordan another constituency to navigate as he builds his leadership operation.
  • "The reason he's the minority leader is he's built relationships all across the conference, and he's built really meaningful, good relationships. And I have, you know, no doubt that we're going to get a fair shot here," Flood said.

What they're saying: Freedom Caucus members oppose Main Street's proposal.

  • "It's not going to happen," outgoing HFC Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) told Axios. "They introduce it every year."
  • "That's inappropriate," Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga) told Axios of Flood's original proposal. Clyde also told Axios he doesn't think the proposal will get anywhere, saying that he thinks enough feel the same as he does to kill it.

Reality check: With Republicans headed into one of the smallest minorities in recent history, the changes would have little effect in the upcoming Congress.

But members want to settle the conference's accountability rules now, so when they regain the majority, the same divisions won't threaten to derail their agenda.

  • "This is us simply setting the table so that when we do return to the majority, we can do so built on a foundation that addresses some of the hiccups we experienced during the 119th Congress," Flood told Axios.
  • "We're in the minority now, this is the time to set the rules. This is the time to get this thing right," one GOP lawmaker told Axios. "The goal is to take away the ability of an extremely small group to extort leadership," the member added.
  • "There needs to be consequences for those who choose not to play as a team. What's doubly frustrating is many of those who choose not to be good teammates rarely attend caucus meetings or are willing to negotiate within the tent. Too often, they are the ones talking to reporters on the steps," another GOP lawmaker told Axios.

What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to meet in December to consider changes to conference rules.

item.title: United Airlines resolves "widespread system outage" that delayed flights
item.description:
United Airlines said Monday that it resolved what it called a "widespread system outage" that delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes.

Why it matters: It was a quick resolution to yet another issue affecting the U.S.' beleaguered airspace, which spent days digging itself out of thousands of flight delays and cancellations following Friday's hours-long ground stop.

What they're saying: "We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United Airlines wrote on X in reply to a customer.

  • "We appreciate your patience while we work through this. Please check back with us for updates, and keep an eye on your flight status through the United app or at http://united.com. Thanks for bearing with us!"
  • The customer said the issue stemmed from planes being unable to determine weight limits, though United did not confirm that was the problem.

United Airlines told Axios that the company is "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights."

  • "There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights. There is no indication that this is a cybersecurity-related issue," they said.
  • About an hour and fifteen minutes after United posted its apology, the company tweeted again to say the issue was resolved and encouraged passengers to check their flight status at the company's website.
  • United gave no additional information about what caused the outage, and it's unclear how many flights were impacted.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

item.title: Fewer international students, billions at stake
item.description:
Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns.

Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students.

  • Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce.

Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education.

  • Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students.
  • International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates.
  • However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%.

Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios.

  • She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities.
  • "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues."
  • Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships.

By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars.

  • Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators.
  • That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported.
  • It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth.

Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that declining international enrollment left apartments vacant and affected plans to build more student housing.

Between the lines: Spreitzer attributes some of the declining enrollment to the Trump administration's immigration policies.

  • International students "are trading horror stories about being stopped at the border," she says, adding that fears of being denied re-entry is too big of a risk.
  • Eighty-eight percent of institutions reporting declining enrollment cited the visa application process, while 70% cited travel restrictions, per a separate IIE report.

Zoom in: Smaller institutions, particularly in the Midwest and away from the coasts, may be experiencing much sharper declines than prestigious universities with stronger international name recognition.

  • Spreitzer contrasted the potential experiences of elite institutions like Harvard with smaller liberal arts colleges that have relatively few international students.
  • A school like Harvard has a massive endowment to help cushion the blow, but others are going to have to make sacrifices.

Case in point: At the University of North Texas, the university is phasing out dozens of minors, cutting four master's programs and merging multiple departments to address a projected $45 million deficit.

  • The university has among the highest numbers of international students in Texas, but the declining enrollment is substantially lowering revenue.

The bottom line: Universities aren't just losing students for one semester. They're potentially losing years of enrollment, tuition revenue and future research talent.

  • "If that student doesn't come this year, that means we've lost out on many years of their enrollment," Spreitzer says. "So this is going to have a cascading effect."

Go deeper: What to know about the wave of student visa cancellations

item.title: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop
item.description:
A newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop last Friday, which disrupted thousands of flights nationwide.

Why it matters: The technical failure exposes vulnerabilities in the FAA's aging telecommunications network, raising questions about how a technical failure could trigger a nationwide ground stop and disrupt air travel.

Catch up quick: More than 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, the FAA said, with thousands more delayed.

  • "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Sunday.

Read more below.

What caused the nationwide groundstop?

What they're saying: The FAA says its network was flooded with data "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds," causing "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds."

  • Investigators tracked the data traffic surge to two possible locations — a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, per the Wall Street Journal.
  • The FAA says its network service provider, L3Harris, has been deploying a new router at the Arkansas facility, which is why it's under investigation for potentially disrupting flights nationwide.

After L3Harris blocked network traffic from both facilities, the system stabilized, allowing normal flight operations to eventually resume, per the FAA.

  • "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the company said in a statement.

How did a router disrupt flights nationwide?

How it works: Air traffic controllers speak with pilots over radio frequencies and receive radar information used to track aircraft.

  • The network connects air traffic control facilities and carries communications and radar information that controllers need to safely manage aircraft.
  • A router directs data traffic across a network. Any disruption could send swaths of data across the system, potentially disrupting communications.

The FAA says a massive surge of data may have overwhelmed the old equipment, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds.

  • The disruption reportedly impacted more than half of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which primarily handle high-altitude flights.

What to know about radio frequency outages

One symptom of the wider network instability: radio frequency disruptions.

  • Some reports described this as a "rolling frequency outage," where disruptions affect different radio frequencies and plane-monitoring facilities at the same time.
  • This could cause planes to lose contact with the air control centers.

Reality check: Losing contact with air traffic controllers can complicate the instructions pilots rely on to navigate crowded airspace safely. It doesn't mean they're flying completely in the dark, but it can make air travel and airspace management messy.

What happens to pilots during the outages?

Zoom in: The FAA normally has backup systems and procedures designed to keep communications going when radio frequencies fail.

  • These include backup radio transmitters and receivers at air traffic control centers, per the FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual.
  • The FAA says switching to a backup radio system seldom takes more than 60 seconds during a typical frequency outage.
  • Pilots who lose communication with their controllers can also try to reach controllers through alternative frequencies or by contacting specific facilities.

Yes, but: Backup systems don't eliminate the safety concerns posed by widespread communications failures, particularly when multiple air traffic control facilities are affected.

What does this mean for flights?

Zoom out: The nationwide ground stop ended Friday after massive flight delays and cancellations, but airlines have continued to experience schedule disruptions.

  • Departing flights were grounded for several hours, with about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landing safely, per reports.
  • Delays and cancellations continued as airlines worked to reposition crews, staff and aircraft.

What's next: The FAA says it will investigate the cause of the disruption with L3Harris.

  • The agency says it has disabled the relevant broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers to prevent another disruption.

item.title: SCOTUS gives DEI a boost after national assault
item.description:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear three conservative appeals tied to battles over diversity, equity and inclusion, leaving lower-court rulings intact in disputes over federal research grants, medical training and transgender-related speech.

The big picture: The denials mark a reprieve after years of backlash against DEI, though the justices stopped short of settling the underlying constitutional debates.

  • One of those Monday decisions set back President Trump's administration push to cancel swaths of DEI-related research grants.

Driving the news: The justices rejected President Trump's bid to revive cuts to federal research grants awarded to University of California researchers over their perceived DEI-related viewpoints.

  • A U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel ruled in May that challengers were likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim that their grants were terminated because of the "perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints."
  • That decision partly upheld a preliminary injunction from U.S. District Judge Rita Lin reinstating grants terminated over perceived DEI-related viewpoint, while reversing relief for a separate group.

What they're saying: Trump's DOJ argued to the high court that allowing the grants to continue would force taxpayers to fund ideologies "their public stewards reject."

  • A DOJ spokesperson told Axios the department will continue fighting the preliminary injunction and "will continue to advocate for the Executive Branch's lawful authority to administer federal funding programs and for the termination of taxpayer-funded DEI initiatives."

Catch up quick: The challenged funding represents just a slice of the DEI-related grants ensnared in the administration's terminations and ensuing litigation.

  • Trump has led a top-down campaign to undermine federal and corporate DEI efforts, disputes over state policies have also crept onto the national stage.

Case in point: The Supreme Court also declined to hear a challenge from the anti-trans Gays Against Groomers against Colorado lawmakers' restrictions on misgendering and deadnaming during legislative hearings.

  • The Tenth Circuit had found lawmakers were shielded by legislative immunity.

Meanwhile: The justices also declined to hear a challenge to required implicit bias training for California continuing medical education courses.

  • Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated he would've heard the appeal brought by an ophthalmologist and a conservative medical advocacy group. Justice Clarence Thomas penned a dissent, joined by Justice Samuel Alito.
  • Thomas' argument indicates there may be an appetite for a similar question about government speech in the future: "A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny," he wrote.

What we're watching: Both in the courts and in the public arena, disputes over the federal administration and state leaders' handling of DEI initiatives are still playing out with many more sure to come.

  • But on Monday, a high court that hasn't always sided with DEI initiatives declined to further some key debates — for now.

Go deeper: Trump says he "ended DEI." Courts disagree

item.title: Exclusive: White House requires signoff before staffers testify to Congress
item.description:
The White House counsel has instructed all executive branch agencies to get permission from their chief legal counsel and legislative affairs offices before allowing any employee to testify before Congress, according to a memo obtained by Axios.

Why it matters: Monday's memo from White House Counsel Will Scharf is the latest sign President Trump is ready to fight the many investigations being promised by Democrats, who will have significant majorities in both chambers of Congress in January.

  • "The Trump administration will not be extorted, intimidated, or threatened into submission by politically motivated baseless investigations," a White House official said.

Zoom in: Scharf's memo to staffers follows a letter he sent last week to the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif). In that letter, Scharf warned Democrats to limit their investigations to "legitimate" inquiries.

  • "The Supreme Court has held that '[i]nvestigations conducted solely for the personal aggrandizement of the investigators or to 'punish' those investigated are indefensible," Scharf warned.
  • "Congressional investigations must further a legitimate legislative task; Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary," the letter said.

Between the lines: Partisans will likely differ on what's "legitimate," but it's clear that Scharf's office will use its interpretation in deciding whether to allow executive branch employees to testify.

  • "We are ready to engage with Congress," the White House official said, "This process ensures reasonable requests are respected, but baseless political attempts to undermine our mission will not be accepted as the status quo by Democrats' who want to slow the administration down from its historic work."
  • In his Monday memo, Scharf said the administration "will remain disciplined in pursuing the work and service the American people deserve by ensuring that all Executive Departments and Agencies follow the established White House consultation process ... before any agency personnel may agree to appear before any congressional committee."

Zoom out: For more than a year, Trump's administration has planned for the day congressional investigations ramp up.

  • Trump knows he also faces the prospect of impeachment. But advisers say that's no longer threatening to Trump, and he doesn't believe there would be the 67 votes needed in the Senate to remove him.
  • "The president can count, and he won't be cowed," a Trump adviser said.
  • Trump also has promised to pre-emptively pardon staffers and allies he believes will be unfairly targeted by Congress or prosecutors in future Democratic administrations.

The White House counsel has instructed all executive branch agencies to get permission from their chief legal counsel and legislative affairs offices before allowing any employee to testify before Congress, according to a memo obtained by Axios.

Why it matters: Monday's memo from White House Counsel Will Scharf is the latest sign President Trump is ready to fight the many investigations being promised by Democrats, who will have significant majorities in both chambers of Congress in January.

  • "The Trump administration will not be extorted, intimidated, or threatened into submission by politically motivated baseless investigations," a White House official said.

Zoom in: Scharf's memo to staffers follows a letter he sent last week to the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif). In that letter, Scharf warned Democrats to limit their investigations to "legitimate" inquiries.

  • "The Supreme Court has held that '[i]nvestigations conducted solely for the personal aggrandizement of the investigators or to 'punish' those investigated are indefensible," Scharf warned.

item.title: U.S. attorney targets another Democrat over congressional investigtions
item.description:
A U.S. attorney put likely incoming Senate Banking Committee Chair Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on notice about her intent to investigate corporations and expected probes into the president's inner circle.

Why it matters: The letter demanding Warren preserve documents related to her congressional oversight is the latest in a string of threats levied against congressional Democrats ahead of the party assuming the congressional majority — and gavels — next year.

  • Congress' authority to investigate, hold hearings and gather testimony is a core legislative power. Analysts have long forecasted a Democratic subpoena storm into President Trump's lucrative presidency.
  • But Democrats' plan to exercise that power and hone their focus on the administration's "cost, chaos and corruption," as reported by Axios' Hans Nichols, is already facing Justice Department pushback.

Driving the news: U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of the Southern District of Texas contended in his Sunday letter that Warren appeared "eager to wield" her "gavel like a tomahawk," instructing her to preserve oversight records.

  • In the strongly worded letter, he warned Warren about targeting private citizens close to the president and reiterated that any probes must serve a legislative purpose or risk violating those individuals' First Amendment rights. Those arguments echo his prior letters to Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.).
  • Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, shared Reitz's letter and referenced two civil rights statutes. Warren's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Zoom in: Reitz's letter referenced Warren, Blumenthal and incoming Oversight chair Rep. Robert Garcia's (D-Calif.) recent inquiry into Trump fundraiser Meredith O'Rourke's role in coordinating contributions for the president's ballroom and other projects.

  • It also referenced letters Warren, with Slotkin and other lawmakers, sent to tech CEOs probing the extent to which their AI investments were subsidized by GOP-led tax breaks.

What they're saying: The White House did not respond to detailed questions but referred Axios to White House counsel Will Scharf's letter to Garcia that argued Democratic threats of investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

  • Asked if Warren was the subject of a criminal probe or other proceedings, a Justice Department spokesperson told Axios that "the Department does not confirm or deny the existence of ongoing investigations."
  • "The Department has both the statutory authority and the responsibility to examine potential violations of the law," the spokesperson added.
  • Asked if DOJ leadership authorized or reviewed the letter, the DOJ referred Axios to Attorney General Todd Blanche's prior statement that "DOJ leadership is working with every U.S. attorney, including U.S. Attorney Reitz, on ongoing investigations."

Friction point: Blanche refused to rule out prosecuting Democrats set on investigating administration officials in an interview earlier this month, claiming lawmakers' rhetoric had overstepped their authority.

  • That came after Trump demanded the DOJ look into what he labeled as "Weaponization and Lawfare" from his political opponents.

What we're watching: Reitz asked Warren to respond to his letter by next Monday. He described the letter as his "first arrow shot."

Go deeper: Corporate America's Trump trap

item.title: Average diesel prices are under $6 per gallon for the first time in months
item.description:
Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios

Average U.S. diesel prices inched below $6 per gallon on Monday for the first time since Sept. 10 amid lower oil prices recently, per AAA data.

Why it matters: Diesel soared even more than gasoline during the Iran war, and those costs rippled throughout the economy.

  • Democrats featured high prices, especially for farmers, en route to midterm wins in typically red agricultural states.

Zoom out: The worldwide diesel supply crunch remains acute even as the broader oil market is starting to fitfully stabilize.

  • Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, damage to Middle Eastern production and shipments, throttled oil supplies, and expanded U.S. exports to meet overseas demand helped raise domestic costs.

The bottom line: Prices are now far below the Sept. 22 record of nearly $6.53 per gallon. The recent relief is real, but it's limited.

  • Average U.S. prices remain well above the prior record $5.82 per gallon set in 2022.

item.title: Employer health cost crunch is worse than projected
item.description:
There's new evidence that double-digit health cost increases were hitting employers well before the forecasts of big spikes for 2027 — forcing big changes in workplace coverage for millions of Americans.

Why it matters: The findings offer a higher-resolution view of how much health spending is putting a drag on the labor market and increasing affordability concerns for the approximately 160 million Americans who get coverage through work.

  • They also show how factors like surprise billing disputes, more cancer diagnoses and expensive specialty drugs are combining to exert cost pressure, with no immediate relief in sight.

Driving the news: A new Gallagher benefits survey of more than 3,700 firms found 36% of the companies reported premium increases of 10% or more during their most recent renewal.

  • Pharmacy costs account for a quarter or more of some companies' total health spending.
  • Cancer care is the No. 1 cost driver for about 7 in 10 firms.
  • The survey, fielded from January to March, also found employers are trying to avoid saddling workers with a disproportionate share of rising costs while struggling to balance the quality of care with their financial risk.

"The last two renewal cycles have been unlike anything we've ever seen before," said Robby White, Gallagher's U.S. benefits business line leader. "It's unsustainable, obviously. Every additional dollar that an employer spends on health care, they can't spend on their employees."

Between the lines: The 2027 coverage year was already shaping up to be painful for many employers. Projections are showing premium spikes due to rising demand for health services, more chronic disease and increased use of drugs like GLP-1s.

  • In fact, double-digit premium increases for both the 2026 and 2027 plan years suggest there are more underlying causes, according to benefits experts.
  • One leading factor is chronic disease: More people are being diagnosed with cancer at a younger age, and advanced treatments and related care can result in $10,000 a month in expenses or claims.
  • Drug costs also are surging — and not just because of demand for GLP-1s. The high cost of specialty drugs for chronic or rare conditions is prompting companies to scrutinize the way formularies are designed and how well pharmacy benefit managers administer their benefits.

White said another big cost driver is the No Surprises Act, which shielded consumers from large, unexpected medical bills but also created an expensive arbitration process.

  • The arbitration has added administrative costs and is giving providers big payouts, which add millions in costs for large employers that self-fund their health plans.
  • That's an assessment shared by big health insurers, which say the surprise billing law is creating unintended financial consequences.
  • "The [independent dispute resolution] process has now become a top-three single driver of health care cost increases for employers," Aetna president Steve Nelson told Axios, adding the company wants to work with Congress to overhaul the system.

The big picture: In a volatile health market, more employers are self-insuring and directly paying medical claims to have greater visibility and control over health costs, the Gallagher survey finds.

  • As workers get tired of high deductibles, some employers are testing copay-only plans, which vary out-of-pocket costs by medical service and steer workers to providers deemed to be providing the most value. Part of this involves more digital tools to help patients decide.
  • They're also re-evaluating their relationships with pharmacy benefit managers in response to rising drug costs, leading to what White says is a "huge shift" away from the big three PBMs — CVS Caremark, Optum Rx and Express Scripts.
  • On GLP-1s, Gallagher says the question isn't whether the drugs are effective, but whether coverage is financially sustainable. More companies are exploring direct-to-consumer sales through outside vendors and giving employees debit cards or defined subsidies.

What we're watching: Benefits experts are waiting to see how much congressionally mandated changes to PBMs' business practices bring down drug prices and improve transparency.

  • They're also watching the growing number of worker lawsuits against plan sponsors, alleging they breached their fiduciary duty by failing to negotiate reasonable prescription drug prices or keep fees reasonable.

Caitlin Owens contributed to this story.

item.title: The chain-reaction era: Constant shock and awe
item.description:
It was random, but related, that we were hit with a tectonic election result, an epic AI-and-spy scandal, and the dramatic FAA shutdown in just over one week.

  • This is our new reality: constant shock and awe, igniting chain reactions across politics, media, AI, business and culture.

Why it matters: This month's three shocks hit separately. But their speed and spread are our new reality.

Politics, AI, media and business are now one wired system: A jolt in one sets off the other three, instantly.

  • We call this post-processable velocity: Change is moving faster than any person, company, market or government can absorb.
  • People's fears about AI are now mushrooming into jitteriness about civilization's connective tissue. An AP story on Sunday asked: "Could everything be broken?"
  • Images of empty European supermarket refrigerators, cleared of spoiled food after a spate of mysterious cyberattacks, added to the sense that our connections are crumbling, with the simplest conveniences in danger.

What makes all this so disorienting for all of us is how interconnected politics, AI, business and media have become. The Nvidia spy scandal is a vivid example:

  • Media, last weekend: The New York Times reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned President Trump that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang was tied to a suspected Chinese spy. Social media erupts.
  • Business, Monday: Nvidia stock falls more than 4% at the open and keeps sliding. Fears of economy-wide AI fallout follow.
  • Politics, all week: Trump's top team gets dragged into a "what did they know and when" frenzy. Democrats demand hearings.
  • Policy, now: Lawmakers are scrambling to untangle the web of spies, lies and AI, and are racing to tighten China's access to Nvidia chips that gave Huang the power he's now surrendered.
  • Tech, going forward: AI companies are rethinking their reliance on Nvidia chips and exploring financing options beyond Nvidia.

⏱️ Huang's resignation was announced just 14 days after last month's New York Times blockbuster exclusive that he was believed to be the target of a Chinese plot, and four days after he admitted an affair.

  • One revelation, two weeks, and the most important CEO in AI is gone.

Three forces make this permanent:

🔄 1. Politics swings wildly. This was the seventh straight election in which the White House, Senate or House changed hands. And this time, in truly unthinkable and historic ways.

  • There were a number of "split districts" in 2024 that went for Kamala Harris for president and a Republican for the House. This year, every single one swung to electing a Democrat. We can't find any precedent for this.
  • It's possible we've hit a post-ideological age where people feel very little affiliation to party tribes. How do you explain young men shifting almost 40 points from Republicans to Democrats in two years?

🤖 2. AI concentrates everything. A handful of companies are making historic bets on superhuman intelligence, and propping up the economy while they do it.

  • That puts enormous power and risk in very few hands. One man's affair shook the whole market.
  • Nvidia makes the vital ingredient of AI, and helps finance nearly every big player buying it.
  • But it's not just Nvidia. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft or Amazon can rattle the market with one announcement too.

⛓️‍💥 3. Everything is fragile when everything is interconnected. Friday's flight shutdown had nothing to do with AI, spies or elections, but it still shook us all.

  • It appears a contractor was swapping copper wire for fiber. Routers overloaded. Departures stopped nationwide for more than four hours.
  • A total of 18,000+ U.S. flights were canceled over the past three days.
  • Officials said little for hours. Rumors, speculation and gallows humor filled the void. "The aliens have landed," the novelist Stephen King tweeted. "That's the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don't want to start a worldwide panic."

The bottom line: The shocks will change. The speed won't.

  • Go deeper: New signs of rising risk.

item.title: Why Democrats may want to make Trump look good
item.description:
DENVER — Democrats' euphoria over their once-in-a-generation wave of midterm victories is giving way to a reality check:

  • They were lucky to have a weakened opposition. And they might be "renting" this year's voters if they don't quickly deliver on their promises.

Why it matters: If Democrats want to rack up policy wins ASAP, they'll need to work with President Trump — the guy many of them held up as what's wrong with America. That means giving him a few wins.

Zoom in: Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico argued exactly that at a Democratic summit late last week in Denver — What's Next, held by the centrist group Majority Democrats.

  • "If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history."
  • Gina Hinojosa, who'll be Texas' first Democratic governor in more than three decades, has said she'll work with Trump on immigration. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a frequent Trump target, is pitching the president on rebranding Medicare for All as "TrumpCare" to get it passed.
  • And on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told Dana Bash he wants to collaborate with Trump to deliver on the president's own past promise to lower grocery prices.

Zoom out: Midterm elections are usually a referendum on the sitting president, not a sign that voters are in love with the opposition party. And polls show that Democrats are still unpopular.

  • At the Denver confab, several Democrats acknowledged that. Adam Jentleson, president of the moderate Searchlight Institute, said onstage: "The voters who decided last week's election have not yet fallen in love with us. ... They are on loan to us."

Many Democratic leaders believe Congress must prioritize legislation aimed at lowering prices and ending the war in Iran, given the salience of those two issues in this year's elections.

  • Some top Democrats are determined not to repeat the mistakes the party made after the 2022 elections, when they overperformed — and grew complacent. They lost the presidential election two years later.

The other side: Merely talking about working with Trump can disillusion parts of the Democratic base.

  • Outside the Denver event, left-wing activists protested the get-together itself. Some accused Democratic leaders of already being too conciliatory toward the Republican president.
  • "I can't believe that Talarico said he'd work with Trump," Anna Libey, a volunteer for the progressive Sunrise Movement, told Axios. "I can't believe that he would go back on his campaign messaging immediately."
  • (During his campaign, Talarico consistently signaled his willingness to work across party lines, while also routinely criticizing the president's agenda.)

Yes, but: Many Democrats don't really believe Trump will become a serious governing partner overnight, if ever. They just think they ought to be able to say they tried to work with him.

  • If and when Trump vetoes the priority bills of a Democratic-led Congress — as he's already threatened to do — many in the party figure it'd boost their argument that he's still to blame for high prices and his unpopular war on Iran.

  • At the Denver confab, several Democrats acknowledged that. Adam Jentleson, president of the moderate Searchlight Institute, said onstage: "The voters who decided last week's election have not yet fallen in love with us. ... They are on loan to us."

Many Democratic leaders believe Congress must prioritize legislation aimed at lowering prices and ending the war in Iran, given the salience of those two issues in this year's elections.

  • Some top Democrats are determined not to repeat the mistakes the party made after the 2022 elections, when they overperformed — and grew complacent. They lost the presidential election two years later.

The other side: Merely talking about working with Trump can disillusion parts of the Democratic base.

  • Outside the Denver event, left-wing activists protested the get-together itself. Some accused Democratic leaders of already being too conciliatory toward the Republican president.
  • "I can't believe that Talarico said he'd work with Trump," Anna Libey, a volunteer for the progressive Sunrise Movement, told Axios. "I can't believe that he would go back on his campaign messaging immediately."
  • (During his campaign, Talarico consistently signaled his willingness to work across party lines, while also routinely criticizing the president's agenda.)

Yes, but: Many Democrats don't really believe Trump will become a serious governing partner overnight, if ever. They just think they ought to be able to say they tried to work with him.

  • If and when Trump vetoes the priority bills of a Democratic-led Congress — as he's already threatened to do — many in the party figure it'd boost their argument that he's still to blame for high prices and his unpopular war on Iran.

item.title: "No sane person questions whether AI works" — but an AI bubble appears ready to pop.
item.description:
The downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang adds an explosive new risk to an already-strained AI boom, threatening to burst a financial bubble even if the technology ultimately succeeds.

Why it matters: History shows that world-changing technology and devastating financial bubbles often go hand in hand. A market reckoning won't stop the AI revolution. But as with the dot-com crash, it could vaporize trillions in investor wealth as expectations come crashing back to earth.

The big picture: "No sane person questions whether AI works. And that 'working' status is precisely what makes a bubble possible," veteran technology investor Paul Kedrosky told Axios.

  • The risks have grown as technology companies commit trillions to infrastructure, increasingly relying on debt, investments in one another and complicated financing arrangements to keep the expansion going.

Driving the news: Huang's stunning resignation Thursday has shaken confidence in the company at the center of the AI boom — and raised fresh questions about the sustainability of the broader investment frenzy.

  • Nvidia, which named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, faces a leadership vacuum at a time when the industry is already grappling with financial and political uncertainty.
  • Beyond selling chips, Nvidia has helped finance the massive expansion of computing infrastructure by investing in its customers and providing financial backstops for major projects.
  • A more cautious approach by Huang's successor could undermine confidence in projects that have depended on Nvidia's financial support.

What they're saying: RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas told Axios that Huang's departure could trigger a "wholesale bursting" of the AI bubble.

  • "The turmoil around Jensen Huang matters for the buildout if it makes lenders less confident that Nvidia will back the next round of projects," Columbia Business School professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh told Axios.

Zoom out: The financial and political vulnerabilities were piling up well before the Nvidia scandal.

  • Spending is outpacing expected returns. AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, while Gartner forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over the same period, according to Axios reporting.
  • Valuation expectations are being reset. Anthropic's newly announced IPO terms imply a valuation well below earlier hopes of as much as $2 trillion. OpenAI also reportedly secured less cash and a lower valuation than it had hoped in a recent funding round.
  • Investors are growing more cautious. Retail traders, who have routinely bought previous AI-related market dips, instead became net sellers of U.S. stocks during the sharp Nov. 5 selloff, according to Vanda Research.
  • Financing is getting harder. The debt-fueled expansion was already showing signs of strain before the latest turmoil. Rising borrowing costs and an avalanche of new bond offerings have made lenders wary.
  • Political opposition is growing. A wave of election victories for AI-skeptical candidates, along with widespread voter support for data center restrictions, threatens to delay construction, increase costs and undermine the assumptions behind some projects.
  • Regulatory risks are mounting. Huang's downfall has intensified bipartisan demands for tighter restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, which increasingly appear likely to pass.

The risk: A retreat in AI investment could become self-reinforcing, turning a market correction into a much broader financial reckoning.

  • Falling valuations and tighter credit could make it harder for startups and cloud providers to finance additional data centers, reducing demand for chips, power and other infrastructure.
  • That could put further pressure on the investors, lenders and companies financing the expansion, spreading the consequences well beyond the companies developing AI models.

Yes, but: There is considerable evidence that AI itself is a real and potentially transformative technology — and that demand is growing rapidly.

  • Anthropic reported an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, up from $71 billion a month earlier.
  • OpenAI grew quarterly revenue roughly 50% to $10 billion in the third quarter, according to The Wall Street Journal, even as its adjusted operating losses reached $10.9 billion.
  • Businesses are already using AI to write software, automate tasks and perform work that previously required significant human effort.
  • Tighter U.S. export controls could also benefit American AI developers by limiting Chinese rivals' access to advanced computing power, even as they complicate Nvidia's business prospects.

The historical lesson: Some of the greatest technological transformations have been accompanied by speculative investment booms that ended painfully for investors.

  • "I have no doubt that AI will be transformative. That does not preclude a financial bubble," MIT economics professor Ricardo Caballero told Axios.
  • Caballero argues that excessive optimism may even be necessary to marshal the enormous investments required for a new technology to reach its potential.
  • Such booms can leave behind valuable infrastructure and lasting economic gains, as they did in the dot-com boom-bust cycle, even if many investors suffer losses along the way.

The bottom line: "AI can deliver enormous value to users while the companies building the infrastructure earn far less than their investors expected," Van Nieuwerburgh said.

item.title: MAGA figures hope Jensen Huang's spy scandal finally breaks Trump's embrace of Big Tech
item.description:
Prominent conservative thinkers and MAGA figures are seizing on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy to pull President Trump away from his alliance with the tech right.

Why it matters: The Nvidia scandal highlights some of the political weaknesses for Trump in allowing himself to be defined by his connections to an increasingly unpopular group of companies.

  • Right-wing players are hoping the bombshell revelations about Huang's affairs will chip away at the president's embrace of the tech industry and offer an opening for anti-tech voices in his administration.

What they're saying: They view the midterm elections as proof that people across the political spectrum hate AI, data centers and view Silicon Valley as too powerful.

  • President Trump's perception of China "has always been entirely commercial and transactional. His view was, 'we're getting screwed. I'm going to get a better deal,'" Oren Cass, founder of conservative think tank American Compass, said.
  • Cass, who has warned about Nvidia risks for more than a year, said the allegations of espionage are the strongest evidence yet that China is not a commercial partner but an adversary that is going to "subvert the American political process in ways that end up humiliating the President."
  • MAGA figure Steve Bannon, meanwhile, said in a text he has called Jensen Huang "a CCP 'Agent of Influence' a thousand times." and that it's an OPEN SECRET."
  • "We need to actually cut OFF ALL THE CHIPS NOW," Bannon added as Congress warms up to legislation aimed at that.

Reality check: Amid daily revelations about Huang's affairs and the negative consequences for the AI boom and U.S. economy, Trump has created some distance. He backtracked on a suggestion that Jensen could go on a trip to China later this month. Other than that, he has kept it friendly.

  • The president earlier this week called him "honorable" and on Thursday, following Jensen's resignation, the president said he "has done a fantastic job" and called him a "Legend."
  • On Thursday, he said in an interview with Stephen Smith that Jensen is "a tremendous talent" who's done "incredible" and "brilliant" work at Nvidia.

What we're watching: Supporters of Jensen Huang are lobbying the White House to support his reinstatement as CEO, according to the Financial Times.

What's next: Conservatives are hoping the scandal changes who gets a seat at the table for the remainder of Trump's presidency as 2028 and mounting AI unpopularity approaches.

item.title: Dems' Denver victory party previews 2028 battles
item.description:
DENVER — Thousands of Democrats gathered here this weekend for a giddy postelection summit, reveling in their party's historic midterm victories and touting the center-left strategy they say powered them.

  • But some progressives saw the event as a lavish, out-of-touch affair bankrolled by billionaires — exactly what Democrats just campaigned against.
  • "I'm all for celebration, but perhaps a fancy retreat does not exactly meet the tenor of the moment," said Josh Orton, president of the liberal group Demand Justice and a veteran of Bernie Sanders' 2020 campaign.

Why it matters: The competing views of What's Next, the buzzy confab held by the influential centrist organization Majority Democrats, offer an early glimpse of the ideological battles over health care, money in politics and other issues that will define the party's 2028 presidential primary.

Zoom in: Democrats in the Mile High City were practically vibrating with happiness, still not quite able to believe they'd won back both chambers of Congress and flipped deep-red states such as Mississippi and South Carolina.

  • "The vibes are excellent," Delaware Rep. Sarah McBride, a member of the Majority Democrats, said in an interview.
  • "The last high-water mark, we were all in our houses on Zooms," she added, referring to the 2020 presidential election. "This is the first time there's been an undeniable capacity to celebrate widespread wins in the last decade."
  • Free drinks flowed. Political operatives sported bomber jackets embroidered with the phrase "Majority Democrats." Speakers were immortalized in rock concert–style posters on the walls.

For a brief moment in Denver's Mission Ballroom, the often-in-disarray Democratic Party looked united.

  • Several presidential hopefuls downplayed the party's divides in speeches.
  • Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said onstage that ordinary people don't give "a damn" about "where we fall on some imaginary political spectrum."
  • Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin quipped in her address that elected officials who were fighting over progressives vs. moderates had "missed the plot."

The other side: But others in the party weren't interested in all the kumbaya.

  • Young protesters sneaked into the event and heckled House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), shouting "You're a f**king traitor!" while calling for Medicare for All and impeachment.
  • Some audience members were palpably annoyed, yelling "Shut up!"

Another flashpoint emerged over high-dollar donors and super PACs.

  • Majority Democrats — which is largely funded by a billionaire couple and describes itself as an alternative to both the "activist left" and a "gerontocratic establishment" — is already in the crosshairs of the Lever, a progressive publication.
  • Majority Democrats' funding has been the focus of reporting by the Lever. The group tussled with the news site over the Denver event, initially denying it press passes and later blocking one of its journalists from interviewing an elected official.
  • David Sirota, founder of the Lever, said the group's actions were "Trump-like attempts at retribution." But there was a silver lining for the outlet: The back-and-forth generated the single biggest influx of new subscribers in its history, he said.

What they're saying: "What's Next was an overwhelming success: It brought together 3,500 Democrats from across the political spectrum to talk about what worked this cycle and where we go next," said Majority Democrats spokesperson Vidhya Jeyadev.

  • "This cycle, we won seats that had been written off for a generation and proved there is no one way to be a Democrat."

The intrigue: Some potential 2028 candidates in Denver tried to portray themselves as unifiers who can bridge the party's divides.

  • New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim, who declined to rule out a 2028 bid, said, "I understand" where the protesters were coming from.
  • "People are furious," he added.

item.title: Some Dems' 2028 strategy: Make America Nice Again
item.description:
Some Democrats weighing 2028 campaigns for president believe the midterms proved that Americans have soured on Trump-style, scorched-earth political warfare and want a brand of politics that's nicer and more optimistic. Others aren't so sure.

Why it matters: Democrats' midterm blowout has prompted a debate over the lessons of 2026 — whether voters in the 2028 primary will want their own ruthless fighter after two more years of President Trump, or will be itching for a more unifying figure.

Zoom in: That divide was reflected in several potential 2028 contenders' comments around the midterms.

  • Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg told his supporters that the end of the Trump era "means a politics where we can check the news and actually feel our blood pressure come down a little."
  • In his reelection victory speech, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told supporters that "you declared that you could not be more ready for an end of this ruthless chaos and cruelty."

In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom — who led the successful ballot measure to create more Democratic House seats in response to Trump's redistricting push in red states — boasted that California "fought fire with fire."

  • Newsom mocked Democrats who he said would have responded by merely writing op-eds in the New York Times.
  • "Donald Trump is not screwing around, nor are we," Newsom said at a preelection rally, adding that he was proud of leading the "most un-Trump state in America."

The big picture: The midterm results provided an argument for each side.

  • Several key victories for Democrats in red states came from candidates preaching decency, or voters recoiling from vicious Republican attacks.
  • In Kansas, Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said one of his campaign's big ideas was "decency" — and that he wanted to become the "best friend" of Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.).
  • In Ohio, Gov.-elect Amy Acton told her supporters that "basic decency is on the ballot" after her opponent and Vice President Vance defended an attack ad featuring Acton's mother, from whom Acton had been estranged since childhood after accusing her stepfather of sexual abuse.

Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, a seminarian and the first Democrat to be elected statewide in three decades, said that "love my neighbor" informed his approach to politics.

  • In Denver last week at a gathering of Democratic leaders, Talarico pressed the point: "It's been 10 years of this kind of politics — politics as blood sport, politics as trolling and owning and name-calling, politics as professional wrestling. It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all of the time."

The other side: Other Democrats who won key races embraced something like Newsom's edgier approach by pledging to fight fire with fire, and to not unilaterally disarm against Republicans.

  • Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said on the campaign trail that when his opponents go low, he doesn't take the higher ground. He prefers to take them "to the mud and choke them out."
  • He added that too many Democrats "tell you they're fighting, only to show up with a strongly worded letter."

Reality check: Hamilton, Acton and Talarico had unifying messages, but they and their allies also ran tens of millions of dollars in negative ads against their Republican opponents.

  • In 2008, Barack Obama also had a larger theme of change and unity but ran a campaign that unapologetically attacked his opponents.

item.title: Vance may wait until late spring to reveal 2028 plans
item.description:
Vice President Vance won't make a final decision on whether to run for president in 2028 until after the new year — and may wait until late spring to announce his intentions publicly, two sources with knowledge of his plans tell Axios.

Why it matters: Vance remains the early favorite to succeed President Trump as the GOP's presidential nominee, but the party's midterm losses have complicated his political future and could reshape the 2028 field.

  • People familiar with Vance's thinking say he's genuinely undecided about running, and that his decision-making timeline was in place before the midterms. Advisers caution that the timing could change, however.
  • Vance is still discussing a potential bid with his family, including his wife, Usha, following the birth of their fourth child, the sources said.

The big picture: Vance allies say the midterm losses haven't changed his standing as the early 2028 GOP front-runner, citing his donor network, political infrastructure and name recognition.

  • Vance co-founded the secretive Rockbridge Network, which could anchor his presidential fundraising operation. The group met in Houston after the midterms.
  • As Republican National Committee finance chair, Vance has cultivated relationships with major contributors. He also has ties to technology donors Peter Thiel, David Sacks and Elon Musk — the world's richest person and the GOP's biggest financier.
  • Vance campaigned nationwide for the midterms, building relationships with GOP activists and officials who could prove valuable in 2028.

Behind the scenes: Vance's closest political advisers believe he should run in 2028 and that he's likely to do so, according to a person close to the vice president.

But the GOP's midterm losses have given Republicans who want to move on from the Trump administration an opening to argue for a different direction in 2028.

  • Vance likely will have to answer for the Trump administration's record in 2028, potentially complicating his presidential ambitions.
  • Vance privately opposed the Iran war, and some Republicans interpreted his post-midterm criticism of the conflict as an effort to distance himself from Trump's decision to attack Iran.

The intrigue: Republicans close to Vance see Trump's continued presence as another reason to delay announcing his 2028 plans.

  • Vance is wary that launching a campaign too early could shift attention away from Trump and risk alienating him.
  • Trump said that "a lot of people didn't like [Vance's] comments" about the Iran war, but added that he wasn't among them and insisted their relationship wasn't affected.

Zoom in: While Vance weighs a presidential campaign, a few other Republicans are doing so as well — namely Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who's been among the most active Republicans preparing for a potential 2028 run.

  • Cruz's team has held meetings about a possible run, according to people familiar with his operation. But many Republicans, including some Cruz allies, doubt he could seriously challenge Vance, particularly if Trump endorses the vice president.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is viewed by some Republicans as a potentially more formidable rival to Vance.

  • Rubio has attracted support from influential GOP figures, including megadonor Ken Griffin.
  • But Rubio repeatedly has said he would support Vance if the VP were to run, and Rubio's workload as secretary of state and national security adviser has left him without Vance's ready-made political operation.

Other potential Republican contenders include former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

  • DeSantis has been particularly outspoken, calling the GOP's midterm losses a near "extinction-level event" and pointing to Florida's Republican victories as a model for rebuilding the party.

What they're saying: A Vance spokesperson declined to comment.
item.content:encoded:
Vice President Vance won't make a final decision on whether to run for president in 2028 until after the new year — and may wait until late spring to announce his intentions publicly, two sources with knowledge of his plans tell Axios.

Why it matters: Vance remains the early favorite to succeed President Trump as the GOP's presidential nominee, but the party's midterm losses have complicated his political future and could reshape the 2028 field.

  • People familiar with Vance's thinking say he's genuinely undecided about running, and that his decision-making timeline was in place before the midterms. Advisers caution that the timing could change, however.
  • Vance is still discussing a potential bid with his family, including his wife, Usha, following the birth of their fourth child, the sources said.

The big picture: Vance allies say the midterm losses haven't changed his standing as the early 2028 GOP front-runner, citing his donor network, political infrastructure and name recognition.

  • Vance co-founded the secretive Rockbridge Network, which could anchor his presidential fundraising operation. The group met in Houston after the midterms.
  • As Republican National Committee finance chair, Vance has cultivated relationships with major contributors. He also has ties to technology donors Peter Thiel, David Sacks and Elon Musk — the world's richest person and the GOP's biggest financier.
  • Vance campaigned nationwide for the midterms, building relationships with GOP activists and officials who could prove valuable in 2028.

Behind the scenes: Vance's closest political advisers believe he should run in 2028 and that he's likely to do so, according to a person close to the vice president.

But the GOP's midterm losses have given Republicans who want to move on from the Trump administration an opening to argue for a different direction in 2028.

  • Vance likely will have to answer for the Trump administration's record in 2028, potentially complicating his presidential ambitions.
  • Vance privately opposed the Iran war, and some Republicans interpreted his post-midterm criticism of the conflict as an effort to distance himself from Trump's decision to attack Iran.

The intrigue: Republicans close to Vance see Trump's continued presence as another reason to delay announcing his 2028 plans.

  • Vance is wary that launching a campaign too early could shift attention away from Trump and risk alienating him.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is viewed by some Republicans as a potentially more formidable rival to Vance.

  • Rubio has attracted support from influential GOP figures, including megadonor Ken Griffin.
  • But Rubio repeatedly has said he would support Vance if the VP were to run, and Rubio's workload as secretary of state and national security adviser has left him without Vance's ready-made political operation.

Other potential Republican contenders include former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

  • DeSantis has been particularly outspoken, calling the GOP's midterm losses a near "extinction-level event" and pointing to Florida's Republican victories as a model for rebuilding the party.

item.title: Bessent questions did Nvidia "goose" earnings with suspect China chip sales
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO.

Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth.

  • The Treasury secretary casting doubt on the quality of its financial results and leadership could be a blow to an already shaky market.
  • Since the scandal broke open in late October, Nvidia shares have shed more than $1.2 trillion in market capitalization, with impacts on millions of Americans.

Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies.

  • "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said.
  • "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel."

Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance."

  • "This makes me think that as the board conducts the search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company," he said.

For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks.

The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others.

  • In recent days, Bessent has also made clear that the Commerce Department has questions to answer about why it didn't impose tighter controls on Nvidia's exports.
  • As Axios reported earlier this week, administration officials have accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of stalling curbs on Nvidia's exports.

What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

item.title: Trump's border crackdown faces a new blue wall of governors and House members
item.description:
Voters have handed Democrats every House district touching Mexico and all four border-state governorships.

Why it matters: Starting next year, the sweep gives Democrats new leverage over state resources, border spending and legal challenges during President Trump's final two years.

By the numbers: Democrats last held all four governorships — California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas — in January 1979, according to National Governors Association records.

  • 10 for 10: Democrats swept all 10 House districts touching Mexico for the first time since 2008, according to an Associated Press analysis.
  • Three flips: JoAnna Mendoza ousted Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani in Arizona. Bobby Pulido and Katy Padilla Stout flipped Republican-held seats in Texas.
  • Four attorneys general: Democrats also won the top legal offices in all four border states, including Texas, where the party hadn't won an attorney general race since 1994.

State of play: Trump built his immigration crackdown around the southern border. He declared a national emergency on his first day back, expanded the military's role and border barriers, and launched a sweeping deportation campaign.

  • Southwest border apprehensions dropped roughly 91% in the 12 months through August compared with Biden's final 12 months, according to FactCheck.org's October analysis.
  • The crackdown has also reached further into American communities, with ICE arrests surging during the summer of 2026.

Zoom in: Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa's defeat of Gov. Greg Abbott could bring the most immediate border changes.

  • Abbott spent about $11 billion on Operation Lone Star, deploying state police and National Guard troops and building Rio Grande barriers, according to the Texas Tribune.
  • Hinojosa, Texas' first Latina governor-elect, has questioned that spending. She can rethink state deployments and enforcement priorities, though existing laws and federal authority limit her options.
  • Democrats also flipped the Texas House and elected a Democratic attorney general, giving Hinojosa allies in funding and legal battles. Republicans retained the state Senate.

The intrigue: Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed more than 20 lawsuits against Democratic immigration policies and defended Gov. Greg Abbott's border crackdown.

  • His Democratic successor, Nathan Johnson, has vowed to challenge unconstitutional federal border tactics — potentially turning the office from a powerful Trump ally into an adversary.

What we're watching: Several Democrats newly elected to represent border districts in Washington campaigned on both strong border security and pathways to citizenship for longtime undocumented immigrants.

  • Bobby Pulido, who flipped a Texas GOP-held seat, said in his launch video: "Yes, we have to get the criminals out and secure the border. But we can do that without destroying families and our South Texas economy." He also told the Texas Tribune that one of his congressional priorities will be codifying a pathway to citizenship.
  • JoAnna Mendoza, who flipped an Arizona seat, also backs a strong border and legal pathways to citizenship.

That aligns with many border voters' views:

  • An October N+ Univision/YouGov survey found 56% of Texas Hispanic voters thought immigration enforcement had gone too far. Yet 62% wanted border security and a pathway to citizenship for longtime undocumented immigrants pursued together — suggesting Democrats can make gains without abandoning enforcement.

Zoom out: Trump's tariffs and immigration crackdown have rattled businesses that depend on trade and shoppers from Mexico, giving Democratic governors another reason to challenge Washington.

  • Laredo businesses report fewer customers, while merchants near San Diego's border crossings say tougher immigration enforcement has hurt foot traffic and hiring.
  • Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs pressed Washington over tariffs and trade uncertainty. Manufacturers near Santa Teresa, New Mexico, have put projects on hold amid tariff threats and uncertainty over trade rules.

item.title: How Nvidia's scandal knocked thousands off your 401(k)
item.description:
Nvidia's near-30% stock plunge in the last month is a drag on the retirement savings of millions of Americans, many who may not realize just how much their investments are tied to the scandal-engulfed chip giant.

Why it matters: Nvidia's enormous weight in popular index funds means even those who have never purchased a single share of the company could feel the pain of its corporate upheaval in their 401(k)s.

  • The resignation of CEO Jensen Huang after he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy may have cost an average Baby Boomer thousands of dollars, according to an Axios analysis of outside estimates.

By the numbers: Index funds held nearly half of the assets in large private-sector 401(k) plans in 2023, according to the Investment Company Institute.

  • Those funds include investments tracking the S&P 500, and Nvidia accounts for roughly 8% of that index, according to Tom Graff, chief investment officer at financial planning firm Facet.
  • That exposure rises to around 14% in growth-style index funds and can reach 25% to 30% in some technology and semiconductor funds commonly found in retirement plans, Graff said.

Zoom in: For an investor with $100,000 in an S&P 500 fund, a 30% drop in Nvidia shares would knock about $2,400 off the value of that investment given an 8% S&P holding, assuming other stocks in the fund stayed flat.

  • For a growth-style tech fund with 25% exposure to Nvidia, that decline would amount to $7,500 in lost value.
  • An average Baby Boomer holds about $260,000 in their 401(k), according to Fidelity. A tech-style exposure applied to that amount of holdings would equate to about a $20,000 reduction.

Yes, but: Remember, a drop in your investment's value doesn't mean you've actually lost that cash — unless you sell your holdings.

Zoom out: The potential fallout extends beyond Nvidia itself.

  • About 40% of the S&P 500 is tied to the AI buildout, for which Nvidia is central, providing much of the financing and infrastructure needed to fuel the tech boom.
  • If Nvidia's troubles slow the pace of AI data center investment, the damage could spread to other stocks held in Americans' retirement portfolios, analyst Bob Iaccino notes to Axios via message.
  • "A lot of people are starting to realize just how much Nvidia exposure they have in funds they thought were diversified," Graff told Axios. "You don't want too much of your retirement riding on whether Nvidia has a successful transition to new leadership or not," he added.

Reality check: While Nvidia has come to define the AI trade, its competitors have also emerged as potential beneficiaries of the stock's decline.

  • "The mindset has flipped very quickly to 'who might benefit from this?'" Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers told Axios.
  • Chip-company AMD's stock went on a run, rising by more than 30% in a five-day stretch last week, contributing to a broader run in the semiconductor sector. Nvidia makes up a sizable portion of many semiconductor indices and ETFs, showing how rotation can keep bull runs alive even as single stocks falter.
  • Hyperscalers with their own chip ambitions, which at times have looked competitive with Nvidia, have also beaten the growth of the S&P 500 index over the last five days.

Reality check: For those who are direct shareholders, the widely held financial advice would always tell you not to lock in losses as a stock drops.

  • It's very unclear what the investigation will unveil.
  • Nvidia is set to report earnings on Tuesday, giving shareholders more insight into its latest quarterly performance.

The bottom line: Americans don't need to own Nvidia shares directly to have their retirement savings tied to the company's successes, or failures.

item.title: Space data centers could end stargazing as we know it
item.description:
Sprawling networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for humans to stargaze.

  • That's just one of the many risks that come with placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit, according to a new report.

Why it matters: Most Americans don't want data centers built near them, but putting them in space brings a new set of problems.

Threat level: "Companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution," top academic researchers warn in a report for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum, an annual event hosted by the Japanese government.

  • If space data centers proliferate, the "most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night in much of the world could be satellites, not stars," the report said, mirroring astronomers' worries.
  • If the U.S. military adopts the technology, the data centers could become potential targets during future space conflicts.
  • Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around the Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing "risk of collisions" and dangerous space debris.
  • Space data centers are solar-powered, but the vast number of rocket launches needed to put them in orbit generate greenhouse gases and black carbon emissions.

What they're saying: Columbia University's David Sandalow, the report's lead author, told Axios there are still "unknown unknowns" about space data center impacts.

  • "If this is going to happen, it should happen slowly and with care," Sandalow said. "Not just launching lots and lots of these things and, kind of, seeing what happens. ... There's big risks."

By the numbers: Despite those concerns, investors and tech innovators are all in on space data centers.

  • In 2025, around $197 million in investments were tied to orbital data centers, per market research firm Quilty Space. That figure has swelled to $1.11 billion so far this year.
  • SpaceX has applied for a constellation of 1 million data center satellites, according to the Secure World Foundation.
  • Starcloud and Blue Origin's Project Sunrise have ambitions for 88,000 and 51,600 satellites, respectively.

Yes, but: Caleb Henry, Quilty Space's director of research, said that companies may be filing for more satellites than they will likely field. "They don't want to have to bump the number higher up later on," he said in an interview.

  • "We're at a point where people are tallying paper filings as if they are substantive and real," Henry said, "and we just don't know that yet."

The bottom line: Researchers warned that governments and companies need to wait until space data center "risks and impacts are better understood and well managed" before putting them in orbit.
