item.title: Gen Z shatters America's political orthodoxies
item.description:
Young Americans are challenging beliefs their parents and grandparents once considered sacred — from socialism and Israel to Christianity.

Why it matters: Neither party can count on old political loyalties to win over a generation increasingly willing to break with the past.

  • Socialism: 35 years after the Soviet Union collapsed, some 57% of Americans ages 18–34 view socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll. Among Americans 55 and older, 65% view capitalism positively, compared with 34% for socialism.
  • Israel: Decades after Israel fought wars against neighboring Arab states, some 53% of Americans ages 18–34 sympathize more with Palestinians, compared with 23% who sympathize more with Israelis, according to Gallup's February 2026 survey.
  • Christianity: After centuries as the overwhelming religious identity of Americans, only 54% of Americans ages 18–29 now identify as Christian, compared with 76% of those 65 and older, according to nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute's 2025 Census of American Religion, released in April 2026.

Between the lines: The return of forces that voters haven't felt in generations can scramble their priorities all over again.

  • After decades of relatively low inflation, prices surged during the COVID era, with annual inflation hitting 9.1% in June 2022 — its highest rate since 1981.
  • In 2024, young voters who ranked the economy and jobs as their top issue favored Trump by 24 points, according to CIRCLE's analysis of AP VoteCast.
  • Two years later, 78% of financially struggling young students backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 16% for Republicans, according to a November 5 CIRCLE analysis.

State of play: Young voters showed both parties how quickly their support can shift between elections in last week's midterms.

  • Some 66% of voters ages 18–29 backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 31% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE, citing preliminary NORC data.
  • That 35-point Democratic advantage compares with a 14-point margin in the 2024 House election, according to separate Edison Research exit polling.
  • Trump's 2024 gains among young voters, especially men, now look less like a lasting GOP realignment and more like a warning about how quickly younger Americans can change course.

Zoom in: Socialism's fading stigma reached the ballot box in America's two largest cities.

  • Democratic socialists now stand poised to lead New York and Los Angeles after Nithya Raman defeated Karen Bass in Tuesday's mayoral election, joining New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
  • Both built campaigns around affordable housing and inequality, tapping into younger Americans' financial frustrations.

The bottom line: Young Americans aren't necessarily embracing socialism because they've rejected their grandparents' Cold War beliefs, PRRI CEO Melissa Deckman told Axios. They're questioning capitalism because their own economic experiences have left them disillusioned.

  • "What they're seeing isn't working, and the American dream is increasingly out of reach for them," said Deckman, author of "The Politics of Gen Z."

  • In 2024, young voters who ranked the economy and jobs as their top issue favored Trump by 24 points, according to CIRCLE's analysis of AP VoteCast.
  • Two years later, 78% of financially struggling young students backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 16% for Republicans, according to a November 5 CIRCLE analysis.

State of play: Young voters showed both parties how quickly their support can shift between elections in last week's midterms.

  • Some 66% of voters ages 18–29 backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 31% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE, citing preliminary NORC data.
  • That 35-point Democratic advantage compares with a 14-point margin in the 2024 House election, according to separate Edison Research exit polling.
  • Trump's 2024 gains among young voters, especially men, now look less like a lasting GOP realignment and more like a warning about how quickly younger Americans can change course.

Zoom in: Socialism's fading stigma reached the ballot box in America's two largest cities.

  • Democratic socialists now stand poised to lead New York and Los Angeles after Nithya Raman defeated Karen Bass in Tuesday's mayoral election, joining New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
  • Both built campaigns around affordable housing and inequality, tapping into younger Americans' financial frustrations.

The bottom line: Young Americans aren't necessarily embracing socialism because they've rejected their grandparents' Cold War beliefs, PRRI CEO Melissa Deckman told Axios. They're questioning capitalism because their own economic experiences have left them disillusioned.

  • "What they're seeing isn't working, and the American dream is increasingly out of reach for them," said Deckman, author of "The Politics of Gen Z."

item.title: FAA back at "full operations" after Friday outage, Transportation Sec. says
item.description:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that all FAA systems are back to "full operations" after an hours-long outage Friday evening that grounded all air traffic across the U.S.

The big picture: Duffy reiterated his plea to Congress to fund upgrades to the nation's air traffic control equipment, explaining that proper upgrades could have prevented the ground stop.

Driving the news: Duffy explained that the outage was caused when a contractor performed routine maintenance on a telecommunications line to upgrade a copper wire to fiber-optic cable and install a new router.

  • "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down. So we had to switch it over from old copper," Duffy said.
  • Duffy said it's unclear whether the outage occurred because of contractor error or faulty equipment, but they are working to figure that out.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford warned that up to 5,000 flight cancellations will remain throughout today, but airlines have assured the agency that they should return to normal operations by the end of the day Sunday.

  • "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," Bedford said.
  • According to numbers from FlightAware, over 4,700 international and domestic flights have been canceled, and over 13,500 delayed, as of 11:50 am ET.

Zoom out: Bedford and Duffy both said the ground stop was ordered out of an abundance of caution for the safety of passengers and airplane crews.

  • Bedford added that they have no reason to believe a cyberattack or an AI issue prompted the outage.
  • "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious," Bedford said.

Zoom in: Duffy used the press conference to again plead with Congress to fund upgrades for the aging air traffic control system.

  • Duffy has previously said the FAA needs $30 billion to update airports and air traffic control. Congress had previously awarded $12.5 billion in July 2025 for upgrades into 2030.
  • After Friday's outage, Duffy upped the funding request to $50 billion.
  • "For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it, and the president is pushing it, but we don't get the resources," Duffy said. "And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait, America and Congress? And I think this is a sign for them to lean in. This is bipartisan."

Bedford offered a blunt assessment when reporters asked about the system's function, saying it's the "worst-kept secret in government" that it needs an upgrade.

  • "We have to keep the existing system operating at the very best of our ability," with the funding they have, he said.
  • "But," Bedford continued, "let's not kid ourselves. It will continue to break until we replace it."

item.title: AI's four colliding crises
item.description:
AI's titans were handed an extraordinary mandate: Police yourselves.

  • But the industry faces a four-pronged crisis of trust as Democrats surge to power and many Americans rebel over AI and data centers. Guardrails for the industry will be a priority for the new Congress, with some populist Republicans eager to pile on.

Why it matters: The collision of safety scares, political blows, financial turmoil and leadership scandals threatens to derail AI's once seemingly unstoppable ascent.

The big picture: Just six weeks ago, President Trump announced that top AI CEOs had agreed to a voluntary safety accord.

  • But cracks were already showing and, since then, four crises have converged.

🏛️ 1. The political crisis: AI was on the ballot for the first time during the midterm elections through a series of data center measures across America. People voted against data centers in 40 out of 41 cases, and swing-state incumbents linked to the facilities, including Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), were voted out.

  • Now Democrats are planning a flood of AI bills once they take control of Congress in January, Reuters reports. They'll also bring some of the most powerful AI executives to D.C. to testify.

🦺 2. The safety crisis: OpenAI's Hugging Face breach, revealed in July, was a terrifying look at what could happen if machines operate beyond humans' control — and it was the first in a wave of revelations through the summer and fall.

  • AI CEOs and engineers came forward with stark warnings about the dangers of the tech they've been building, including its potential to destroy humanity.
  • Axios' Madison Mills reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of security incidents and that unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts.

💰 3. The financial crisis: The AI trade is looking more vulnerable as investors question when or whether the industry's sky-high spending will deliver sky-high returns.

  • Tech stocks tumbled, with Nvidia falling 13% this week amid the ouster of founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The stock has lost nearly 25% of its value since the first New York Times report in late October about Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy.
  • Anthropic's IPO may not be what some hoped, with its projected valuation coming in roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago.

🧐 4. The leadership crisis: Huang's stunning resignation, following revelations about affairs, is raising new questions about the vulnerability of the people running America's most powerful companies.

  • Nvidia's stock slide exemplifies the risk of putting so much power in the hands of so few AI executives.
  • Pop culture has turned on the AI titans, with three year-end films — "The Social Reckoning" and "Musk," out last month, and "Artificial," opening Christmas Day — savaging Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Reality check: The AI industry's hurdles are partly growing pains — investors start demanding returns, lawmakers seek accountability, the public grows skeptical.

  • The trust collapse echoes the moment social media companies went from Silicon Valley darlings to public enemies. But AI's reckoning — just like its rise — has come much faster.

item.title: MAGA turns on Lutnick amid China spy scandal
item.description:
Commerce Secretary Lutnick has become the face of the Trump administration's troubled response to Chinese espionage and potential national security threats.

  • The most intense scrutiny is coming from Republicans on the Hill, fellow Cabinet members and the MAGA base.

Why it matters: Regulators and policymakers on both sides of the aisle want someone's head for an affair that may have exposed sensitive technology to the nation's top foreign adversary.

  • Two names are currently at the top of that list: former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — and now Lutnick.

The big picture: Over the past year, Lutnick slow-walked broader administration efforts to address suspicions that Singapore-based company Megaspeed was illegally diverting chips to China, Axios first reported.

  • Administration officials had pushed to place Megaspeed on the Commerce Department's Entity List, which would have restricted exports of U.S. tech to the company.

Driving the news: On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed as much.

  • "Treasury, War, USTR, and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC.
  • Trump himself supported taking action on three occasions, but those efforts were delayed by Lutnick, Axios reported.

There's a widespread belief in Trump's broad circle of advisers that the Nvidia scandal might be too much for Lutnick to survive — but Trump is standing beside him for now.

  • Behind the scenes, the White House has not expressed concern regarding efforts to have Lutnick testify before Congress.
  • MAGA commentators are also tearing Lutnick apart on shows like "War Room with Steve Bannon," while Republican senators openly take him to task.

For the record: "Secretary Lutnick plays a fundamental role in advising the President across many different industries. The reports you have issued are inaccurate and false and literally misstate the topic, creating a false impression," the Commerce Department said in response to Axios' inquiries.

Friction point: The brewing scandal hangs in part on a CIA warning that Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, who ran Megaspeed and was also alleged to be a Chinese spy.

  • That warning appears to have been ignored by Commerce Department officials, sources told Axios.

Context: Last fall, CIA intelligence indicated Huang was the target of the espionage, which was reported in a "book" assembled by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence for a small circle of administration officials with top secret clearance, according to sources familiar with the matter.

  • In March, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who's also White House national security adviser, compiled a memo about the issue to ensure that Cabinet officials with "equities" in Nvidia and AI were informed, one of those sources said.
  • "The memo was made so that Lutnick and Bessent and others knew what was up," said one source.
  • "Howard was given the memo. He ignored the memo," a second source said.

In May, as Trump traveled to China aboard Air Force One, Rubio verbally briefed the president as a "reminder," one of the sources said.

Reality check: Through it all, Trump has repeatedly been in Lutnick's corner.

  • The president has defended Lutnick time and again, whether over tariffs, immigration or the latest China tussle.
  • There are no indications Trump has changed his stance since publicly defending Lutnick on Thursday.

The bottom line: While Trump continues to defend Lutnick, administration officials and congressional Republicans have clearly picked a target.

item.title: Wholesale food prices are on the rise
item.description:
Food prices are rising sharply even before they reach supermarket shelves.

Why it matters: Americans are already paying more for groceries. New inflation data this week suggests that the pressure is not letting up.

  • Wholesale fresh and dry vegetable prices surged 27% last month, adding to a 31% price jump the previous month.
  • These are the prices paid by food distributors, grocery chains and other businesses to farmers and other producers for eventual sale to consumers.
  • Wholesale food prices overall are up 1.7% from a year earlier, ending a three-month streak of annual price declines.

Zoom in: Unusually warm weather, crop disease and insect infestations have reduced lettuce and other leafy green harvests in California.

  • The Iran war, meanwhile, has driven up the cost of fertilizer and fuel, making it more expensive to grow and transport food.
  • A regional grocery chain recently told Federal Reserve officials that it now costs more to transport a head of lettuce from California than to buy the lettuce itself, citing high diesel fuel prices.
  • Truck freight costs are up almost 25% over the past year, the largest annual increase since 2022 and on par with the surge seen during the pandemic-era inflation shock.

The big picture: It's unclear how much of the surge in producer prices will be passed along to consumers. But steeper price increases were already showing up at supermarket checkout counters last month.

  • Grocery prices rose 0.4%, the biggest monthly increase in 6 months, driven by higher prices for meat, dairy products and snack foods.
  • Fresh vegetable prices climbed 2%, including a nearly 8% jump in lettuce prices.

item.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status
item.description:
An international health organization has determined that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, according to multiple news reports.

Why it matters: It's an official recognition of how much the country's public health has deteriorated due to a rolling series of outbreaks since early last year.

  • Increased public skepticism about the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, a barrage of distrust from federal officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and funding cuts for response efforts have all factored in the surge of cases, according to public health experts.

The big picture: The Pan American Health Organization concluded there has been sustained transmission of the highly contagious virus for longer than 12 months, bringing the U.S. case count to its highest level in 35 years.

  • The measles elimination status hinges on whether the same strain of measles stays in circulation for 12 months or longer without a break.
  • The overwhelming majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. While overall measles vaccination rates remain relatively high, public health officials say they have to remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity.

Driving the news: An expert panel convened by the Pan American Health Organization made the widely expected decision following a three-day meeting in Washington, D.C.

What they're saying: "It is no surprise that the resurgence of measles has coincided with an administration that has inflicted significant damage to our health care system while spreading false claims about vaccines," said Richard Besser, president and CEO of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and a former acting director of the Centers for Disease Control.

  • "It is unthinkable that people in the United States should be dying from measles in 2026," the Infectious Diseases Society said in comments prior to the decision.
  • The group cited the potential long-term toll on infants infected this year, some of whom could develop serious neurologic disease years after the initial infection.

By the numbers: There have been 5,412 confirmed cases so far this year, compared to 2,289 for all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's latest tally.

  • The last time measles cases were higher was in 1991, when the U.S. had 9,643 cases.
  • Pennsylvania is in the grip of an outbreak that has accounted for more than 1,500 cases so far and six measles-associated deaths.
  • Those reports are widely considered to be an undercount, due to the lack of widespread testing and unreported instances of mild illness.

While most measles cases aren't severe, they can have long-lasting effects because of the way the virus can suppress the body's immune responses, leaving people more susceptible to other infections.

  • About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles is hospitalized, per the CDC.

How it works: Experts rely on disease tracking by local health departments and genetic sequencing, and can also factor vaccination rates and surveillance efforts.

  • Canada and the United Kingdom have both lost their measles elimination status over the past year.
  • The determinations are largely symbolic, but mean the virus has become endemic and is spreading freely in pockets of unvaccinated people, according to Yale epidemiologist Katelyn Jetelina.
  • Since early 2025, there have been large-scale outbreaks in West Texas, along the Utah-Arizona border and in South Carolina.

item.title: 3,000 flights cancelled as FAA ground stop chaos stretches into 2nd day
item.description:
The chaos from the FAA's nationwide ground stop lingered into early Saturday morning, with thousands of flights cancelled as airlines played catch-up.

Why it matters: Millions of travelers will find themselves inconvenienced over what the government says was simply old technology that couldn't keep up with modern upgrades.

Driving the news: As of 5:15 a.m. ET Saturday, nearly 3,300 flights into, out of, or within the United States were already cancelled for the day, per FlightAware.

  • Nearly 1,000 flights already had delays.

Between the lines: The most heavily impacted airports were Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson, New York's JFK and Boston Logan.

  • Among the major airlines, FlightAware's data showed Delta more affected than United or American.

Zoom in: The ground stop wreaked havoc on college football in particular, with many schools unable to travel to their game locations.

  • ESPN reported a number of high-profile match-ups were postponed to either late Saturday or Sunday as a result.

What to watch: Whether Congress responds to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's request for $50 billion in emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: FAA ends hours-long nationwide ground stop
item.description:
The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday night after hours of chaos and thousands of delays and cancellations.

Why it matters: The effects of the rare and extreme move will likely ripple through the weekend, with travelers stranded and airlines' planes and crews out of position.

Driving the news: In a Friday evening press conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was issued after outdated air traffic control communications equipment suffered from "overloaded data, and they went down."

  • Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin added that officials are looking into incompatibilities between that older equipment and newer technology currently being installed.
  • Mullin added that there's no evidence that the problems were tied to a cyberattack.

Yes, but: Duffy and Mullin didn't specify the exact initial cause of the problems.

  • "We're still working on the details of what went wrong today," Duffy said.

Duffy spent much of the press conference pushing Congress for more funding for air traffic control upgrades.

  • "I can't build things if I don't have money," he told reporters at the White House briefing room.
  • He later added that similar problems could occur again without more funding.

Catch up quick: The FAA initially issued the stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety."

  • "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the agency said in an earlier statement after the ground stop was issued.
  • "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates."
  • Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often simply called "centers," mostly handle high-altitude en route airspace between airports.

Between the lines: The FAA has been rolling out a new AI tool designed to help manage airspace congestion, but it's unclear if that system has any connection to Friday's communication issues.

  • The developer of that tool denied any connection.

By the numbers: As of 9 p.m. ET, FlightAware reported more than 6,000 cancellations over the course of the day Friday.

  • Many travelers are stuck at the airport or on their planes on the tarmac Friday evening.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with details from a press briefing.

item.title: Mississippi River cruise crash has no fatalities, critical injuries
item.description:
Thirty-two people are in local hospitals and all passengers and crew are accounted for after a tanker collided with a Mississippi River cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans, officials said Friday.

The big picture: With approximately 180 people on the ship, the rescue of all aboard is "truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a press conference.

What they're saying: While the investigation remains ongoing, officials said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker appeared to have lost control, causing it to collide with the cruise ship.

  • As passengers were disembarking after the collision, the cruise ship began to sink and eventually toppled over and flipped — leaving people in the cold water. Video from the scene shows passengers, in life preservers, swimming in the river toward safety.
  • The first 87 passengers got off while the ship was still afloat, Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. She added it "was normal conditions" on the river and that there wasn't a high current, despite how notoriously challenging that stretch of the Mississippi River usually is.
  • "The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said. He added, "I've never been prouder of a group of people than those people that came off of that boat."

Catch up quick: The American Heritage, a vessel operated by American Cruise Lines, had docked for passengers to disembark at the port Friday afternoon about two hours before it was hit, according to a press release from the Port of New Orleans.

  • A city spokesman confirmed to Axios that the riverboat had rolled onto its side in the water, which social media videos appear to corroborate.

Zoom out: The Atlantic Asphalt tanker is registered in the Marshall Islands, and had arrived at the Port of New Orleans on Nov. 11.

  • Per data from myshiptracking.com, the tanker began its current journey in Paulsboro, New Jersey, in late October.

Zoom in: The tanker was immobilized on the river Friday at about 2pm CT, with two tugs positioned on either side.

  • Another dozen vessels were in the water nearby as a helicopter roamed overhead and sirens rang out over the water.

Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

item.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
item.description:
The Trump administration announced a six-month delay Friday in enforcing the Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect in January.

Why it matters: The announcement pauses a set of rules that officials in many states warned they're not ready to handle — and that could cause millions of people to lose their health coverage.

  • A federal court last month struck down a portion of the rules that required chronically ill Medicaid recipients to prove their condition significantly impairs the ability to work in order to qualify for an exemption.

Driving the news: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said Friday there will be an "optional hold harmless period" through June 30 that will give states "a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience."

  • Hospitals have been so worried about the impact of the work requirements that they've created their own outreach campaign to prepare people on Medicaid, per the New York Times.
  • The concern is not that people will be kicked out of the program for not working, but that a chaotic rollout of the requirements will disenroll more people because they don't understand the reporting rules and won't be able to prove they've met the requirements.

What they're saying: "States have made real progress, and they've been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries — at scale and for the long term," said Deputy Administrator and Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman.

How it works: The first-ever work rules mean Medicaid enrollees must report at least 80 hours a month of work, school or volunteering or get an exemption.

  • States were facing tight timetables for setting up systems to notify millions of recipients about the requirements — and to track whether they're complying.
  • Nebraska's early rollout of the work requirements in May led to confusion and coverage denials due to unsubmitted paperwork, per KFF Health News.

What we're watching: Democrats who will control Congress next year intend to push for more delays, or to scrap the work requirements altogether.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with more details on the delay.

item.title: The senators who could join Van Hollen's insurgency against Schumer
item.description:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen is picking up endorsements in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader.

Why it matters: The leadership fight exposes divisions within the Democratic Party days after its sweeping midterm victory, with some demanding a new direction and others crediting Schumer for the historic blue wave.

Driving the news: Van Hollen (D-Md.), a senator since 2017, announced Thursday he's challenging Schumer because "we need new leadership."

  • "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people."

The other side: Schumer has far more public endorsements than Van Hollen.

  • "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?" Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a statement of support for Schumer.
  • Van Hollen has disputed Schumer's claim to credit for the party's midterm performance, arguing that the wave was powered by voters rather than leaders in Washington.

By the numbers: Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen. A candidate will need 28 or 29 votes to win, depending on the outcome of Alaska's Senate race, where votes are still being counted.

Senators backing Van Hollen

State of play: Van Hollen told MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side, though only four have publicly endorsed him.

  • Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night, saying he will fight for working families.
  • Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) threw his support behind Van Hollen when he announced his challenge Thursday.
  • Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) issued an endorsement for Van Hollen Friday afternoon.
  • Incoming Sen. Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) endorsed Van Hollen Friday morning after previously calling for new leadership.

Who wants new leadership?

Some sitting senators have called for a leadership change without endorsing Van Hollen.

  • Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for change but hasn't endorsed either candidate.
  • Before Van Hollen announced his candidacy, Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) told NBC 5 Democrats "absolutely are committed to change," but didn't rule out supporting Schumer.

Several Democratic senators-elect have also called for new leadership:

  • Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.).
  • Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Ill.).
  • Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine).
  • Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.).
  • Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (D-N.H.).

Context: Progressive critics say Schumer hasn't fought hard enough against President Trump and his agenda.

  • Schumer's decision to help advance a Republican-backed government funding bill in March 2025 fueled the progressive backlash against his leadership.
  • The progressive Working Families Party urged Schumer "not to seek another term as Senate Democratic Leader" in a letter, as first reported by Axios. Another labor group has also opposed Schumer and endorsed Van Hollen.

Who's backing Schumer?

Schumer entered the leadership fight with broad support among Senate Democrats.

  • "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader," Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement this week.

Schumer's public supporters include Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and King, along with Schumer himself.

  • Also backing Schumer: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.) and Jack Reed (R.I.).
  • Schumer also received pre-election endorsements from Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), though neither has publicly reaffirmed that support since Van Hollen entered the race.

Senators who haven't picked a side

Several sitting senators have yet to publicly back either candidate.

  • Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) have not publicly committed to either candidate.
  • Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) have called for a caucus debate over leadership.
  • Sens. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) have expressed openness to a leadership change without endorsing either candidate.
  • Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) hasn't committed to Schumer and wants to hear his vision for the Senate.

The 2028 factor

Several potential 2028 presidential contenders face a choice over who should lead Senate Democrats.

  • Ossoff and Booker, both possible 2028 presidential contenders, have yet to pick sides — leaving them to choose between the party's longtime leader and a changing of the guard.
  • Meanwhile, Gallego and Kelly, also seen as possible 2028 contenders, have backed Schumer.

Zoom out: Schumer himself is up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who has also been mentioned as a potential presidential contender.

  • Schumer could also retire rather than seek reelection.

What's next: Senate Democrats will hold a secret-ballot leadership election Dec. 1.

  • Incoming senators will participate, and members can cast their ballots differently from their public endorsements.

item.title: Senate Dems break 32-year drought on leadership challenges
item.description:
As House Democrats barrel toward a speakership coronation, Senate Dems are getting their first contested race for leader in over 30 years.

Why it matters: Democrats have spent years tearing themselves apart over the party's direction — without forcing their leaders to win a head-to-head vote.

  • Senate Democrats will get that fight this year for the first time since Tom Daschle vs. Chris Dodd in 1994 — courtesy of Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) challenging Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).
  • But no one's challenging Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for speaker. The last contested Democratic House leader race was in 2016, when Tim Ryan failed to beat Nancy Pelosi for minority leader.

Between the lines: House Democrats are being bombarded with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, but the two most frequently floated alternatives — Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) — don't appear to want the job.

  • Raskin told Axios that chairing the Judiciary Committee is his "dream job" and that he's "absolutely ... not a candidate for speaker in any way."
  • "I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," Raskin added.

Pressley has privately told colleagues she isn't interested, multiple House Democrats told Axios.

  • "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios.
  • "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership."

The big picture: Since the last contested Democratic leadership election, Republicans have endured the rise of MAGA, former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell's fall from power and a revolving door of House GOP leaders.

  • In 2018, Kevin McCarthy drubbed Jim Jordan 159–43 to become House minority leader.
  • In 2022, McConnell had to beat Rick Scott after the Florida Republican challenged him for Senate GOP leader.
  • In 2023, McCarthy needed 15 ballots to become speaker and was ousted later that year. Republicans burned through nominations on Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan before settling on Mike Johnson.
  • In 2024, John Thune had to beat two challengers — Rick Scott and John Cornyn — to succeed McConnell as Senate GOP leader.
  • In 2026, Jim Jordan ... well, you know what happened. It was Tuesday.

The intrigue: Van Hollen told reporters in Denver on Friday he's stopped "pursuing" a 2028 presidential bid because the "size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call with the American people."

  • Van Hollen is up to five public votes (himself included) ahead of the Dec. 1 secret ballot. Schumer's at 14. The winner will need 29.

Over in the House, the real question at this point feels like whether any House Democrats will oppose Jeffries on the House floor on Jan. 3.

  • Jeffries has enjoyed unanimous support from his caucus since becoming leader in 2022 and is "confident that we're on a positive trajectory" but takes "nothing for granted," he told reporters yesterday.

The bottom line: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill.

item.title: How the Microsoft outage impacted courts and governments
item.description:
Courts and governments worldwide felt the impact of this week's Microsoft outage, which sidelined work and stymied communication.

Why it matters: When Microsoft's popular workplace software went offline Thursday, it meant an extended lunch break for some offices — but for the courts and governments, it raised questions about the vulnerabilities of the technology underpinning justice and governance.

Case in point: The state of Maine's judicial branch warned in a Thursday alert that requests for protection orders filed by email — urgent requests to keep parties safe from harm — may not have been received.

  • Multiple court documents reviewed by Axios show lawyers requesting deadline extensions or alerting judges to the outage impacting their work.
  • That includes DOJ lawyers: Government attorneys asked for an extension in the case brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over President Trump's Kennedy Center takeover, saying the outage prevented them from "completing the necessary coordination."
  • In a separate filing, Beatty's team acknowledged they were impacted as well.

Zoom out: The impacts were also felt in courtrooms and offices internationally.

  • The AP reported that a U.K. criminal trial was delayed as a result, with a Manchester judge saying, per BBC's reporting, "We are learning of the dangers of relying on computers and data systems."
  • U.K.-based police forces also urged the public Friday to call first responders for aid, rather than using online forms.
  • The Supreme Court of the Philippines said it, too, was affected by the outage.

What they're saying: "We obviously need backup methods to keep the wheels of justice turning," says Gissou Nia, the founder and director of the Atlantic Council's Strategic Litigation Project.

  • She pointed to a prior incident that previewed international reliance on U.S. tech: Though not exposed by an outage, the Trump administration's sanctions on the International Criminal Court prompted the Netherlands-based court to move off of Microsoft software to avoid its work being paralyzed.

While court deadlines can be pushed back, service disruption for individuals seeking urgent injunctive relief is more critical, she notes.

  • "If the only way to communicate ... is through these servers, and the request wasn't reached, it can result in somebody having left the country or having moved money out of an account," Nia says.

Reality check: Shay Cleary, a National Center for State Courts consultant who specializes in tech and cybersecurity, emphasizes that courts typically have manual back-up plans in place.

  • "Many of the people who work in courts are dedicated public servants, and they can figure out how to do things right," he adds.

With Congress back in session, Hill communications were also left in a holding pattern Thursday — with one staffer writing on X, "Hope nobody needs Congress for a little while, your Legislative Branch is currently paralyzed by the Outlook outage."

  • Municipal governments in Austin, Texas, and Jacksonville, Florida, among several others, warned that their emails — and in some cases, phone systems — were impacted.

What we're watching: A page providing updates on the suite of Microsoft tech tools said in a Friday morning post that it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress."

  • That statement came some 22 hours after the page first said the company was investigating reports of issues with email access.

The bottom line: The very tools that connect us digitally can also divide us when things go wrong — underscoring the importance of preparing old-school backup plans to fill the gaps.

Go deeper: The internet's hidden security nightmare — and how AI exposed it
item.content:encoded:
Courts and governments worldwide felt the impact of this week's Microsoft outage, which sidelined work and stymied communication.

Why it matters: When Microsoft's popular workplace software went offline Thursday, it meant an extended lunch break for some offices — but for the courts and governments, it raised questions about the vulnerabilities of the technology underpinning justice and governance.

Case in point: The state of Maine's judicial branch warned in a Thursday alert that requests for protection orders filed by email — urgent requests to keep parties safe from harm — may not have been received.

  • Multiple court documents reviewed by Axios show lawyers requesting deadline extensions or alerting judges to the outage impacting their work.
  • That includes DOJ lawyers: Government attorneys asked for an extension in the case brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over President Trump's Kennedy Center takeover, saying the outage prevented them from "completing the necessary coordination."
  • In a separate filing, Beatty's team acknowledged they were impacted as well.

Zoom out: The impacts were also felt in courtrooms and offices internationally.

  • The AP reported that a U.K. criminal trial was delayed as a result, with a Manchester judge saying, per BBC's reporting, "We are learning of the dangers of relying on computers and data systems."
  • U.K.-based police forces also urged the public Friday to call first responders for aid, rather than using online forms.
  • The Supreme Court of the Philippines said it, too, was affected by the outage.

What they're saying: "We obviously need backup methods to keep the wheels of justice turning," says Gissou Nia, the founder and director of the Atlantic Council's Strategic Litigation Project.

  • She pointed to a prior incident that previewed international reliance on U.S. tech: Though not exposed by an outage, the Trump administration's sanctions on the International Criminal Court prompted the Netherlands-based court to move off of Microsoft software to avoid its work being paralyzed.

item.title: Nobody wants to run against Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
item.description:
The movement to prevent House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) from becoming speaker is struggling to get off the ground due to a fatal flaw: Nobody else wants the job.

Why it matters: Despite the phone calls and online petitions, the demands from progressive holdouts, Jeffries' ascent has become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

  • The House Democrats most often floated as potential challengers don't appear to be interested: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) told Axios on Thursday his "dream job" is to chair the House Judiciary Committee.
  • "I am not a candidate for speaker in any way. ... I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," said Raskin.

Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) has privately told colleagues she doesn't want the role despite an online movement seeking to draft her, according to multiple House Democrats who have spoken directly with her.

  • "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios.
  • "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership."

"He's the only one running," Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) told Axios on Thursday when asked if she plans to vote for Jeffries as speaker.

  • Said Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.): "I am really encouraging our leadership to make it easy for me to vote for the one person that's running. But as of right now, there's ... no one else that has put their name forward."
  • "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only person running," said Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.).
  • Jeffries said in a NY1 interview: "Someone could always emerge in the next week or so, but right now there are no declared challengers, no indication that anyone may put themselves forward."

The intrigue: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill.

  • Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) launched his bid to replace Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Thursday night.

Yes, but: The progressive grassroots have continued this week to swamp sitting and incoming House Democrats with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, according to lawmakers and aides.

  • Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) told Axios he has gotten an "avalanche of messages."
  • Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said she is getting "hundreds every day."
  • A senior House Democrat who is supporting Jeffries told Axios the callers into their office have suggested "like 10" different members as possible alternatives.

Jeffries has pushed back on Axios' reporting that members are being flooded with calls, saying in his NY1 interview: "There's no indication that members of Congress have been overwhelmed by any calls."

State of play: Jeffries has begun meeting with skeptics ahead of House Democrats' Nov. 18 leadership elections. He is expected to easily win the nomination for speaker, determined by a simple majority vote of the caucus.

  • The real question is whether any House Democrats will oppose him on the House floor on Jan. 3 and deny him the unanimous support he has enjoyed from his caucus since becoming leader in 2022.
  • "We're going to continue to talk to every single member of the House Democratic caucus, both current members and incoming members, about what we all can do together for the American people," Jeffries told reporters at a press conference on Thursday.
  • The Democratic leader said he is "confident that we're on a positive trajectory" but takes "nothing for granted."

Between the lines: Several Democratic House members and members-elect predicted that, given the grassroots pressure bearing down on progressives right now, at least a handful are likely to openly oppose him.

What they're saying: Leonard told Axios he sat down with Jeffries on Wednesday and shared what he has heard from callers, including "that the Democratic establishment brand is in the toilet and that the leader's name is synonymous with the Democratic establishment."

  • Ramirez said she has "begun conversations" with Jeffries and intends to "have more next week."
  • Asked if Jeffries has met with the Jeffries-skeptic "Bloc" of incoming progressives, she said: "It is my understanding that that they're scheduling time to meet with them."
  • Reps.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) and LaKesha Womack (D-N.C.) said Jeffries met Wednesday with members of the North Carolina delegation, many of whom are holdouts in the speaker election.
  • "We're still having conversations, we're still listening ... at the end of the day, we're going to all sit together, we're going to listen to everything and we're going to move forward like that," said Ojeda.

The bottom line: "I mean, right now, I don't even know if there's anybody that's stepping up against him," Ojeda added.

Editor's note: After this story was published, Kiros clarified that "hundreds" referred to all forms of outreach, including emails (not "hundreds" of calls).

item.title: The global economy's Achilles' heels
item.description:
A defining story of this decade has been a series of global economic shocks: pandemic, war and geopolitical shifts. New research quantifies a rising set of vulnerabilities for the global trade system.

The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain.

  • That manifests partly in physical chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is the one most in the news, but the McKinsey researchers identify a couple dozen others globally, through which 80% of maritime trade passes (although with varying levels of difficulty for shippers to route around).
  • In effect, as the global economy has become more integrated over the last few decades, these vulnerabilities have become more pronounced — which in turn helps explain why the 2020s have brought an ongoing series of disruptive supply shocks.

By the numbers: They find that the share of global imports that face at least two of three major vulnerabilities has risen to 23% in 2024 from 15% in 2000.

  • The list of items with overlapping vulnerabilities includes basic materials like iron ore and more advanced items like lithium-ion batteries, smartphones and memory chips.

What they're saying: "It's not necessarily that trade has gotten less reliable," Tiago Devesa, a co-author of the report, tells Axios. "I think it's more that we have the realization that we actually want to understand what are the potential points of failure, so we can anticipate them."

  • "I think you could make a case that throughout all of these shocks, trade has continued to increase, and trade was actually a very important balancing mechanism," he adds.
  • "It's been increasing precisely in part because we've integrated the fabric of the global economy much more, and in particular, we've led a specialization effort that led to more concentration around the world," says Devesa, a senior fellow at the McKinsey Global Institute.

Reality check: Reducing vulnerabilities and building economic resilience isn't necessarily as simple as relocating a factory.

  • "Some companies just change their suppliers or factory from a geopolitically distant country to a geopolitically closer country, and they think that they achieved resilience," said Jeongmin Seong, a co-author and McKinsey partner.
  • "Even though you change the location of the final assembly, unless you eliminate the risk at this upstream level, you are still exposed."

Between the lines: The steady march of globalization paid major dividends in recent decades in making goods more affordable and powering global growth.

  • Now companies — and governments — are seeking to mitigate the vulnerabilities that system has created and that the last several years made plain to see.

item.title: Inside the aftermath of the Logan Circle shooting
item.description:
It took just minutes for a gunman to shoot six people and upend one of D.C.'s busiest neighborhoods.

The big picture: Thursday morning's violence left one person dead in a Logan Circle gym and five others injured nearby. The gunman later shot himself, police said.

  • The massive police response shut down streets, sent nearly a dozen schools into lockdown and forced residents to shelter in place.

By evening, the streets around VIDA Fitness, where the shooting began, were quiet. Several nearby businesses remained closed, with police tape blocking off storefronts and officers standing watch.

  • Councilmember Brooke Pinto held a vigil. People left flowers and notes outside of the VIDA. "Logan Circle is still a place for love," read one. "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many," read another.
  • But life also carried on: A delivery van unloaded Christmas trees at Whole Foods, and 14th Street bars put out signs advertising happy hour.
Flowers and handwritten notes line the outside of VIDA Fitness. Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios
One note reads: "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many." Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios

What we know: At an afternoon press conference, interim MPD chief Jeffery W. Carroll identified the suspect as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, who lived in the apartment building connected to VIDA Fitness.

  • The man killed was 46-year-old James Stuart, the building's manager and a Northwest D.C. resident, Carroll said.
  • Police believe the shooting was linked to an ongoing dispute between Lambert and his condominium association over maintenance issues, including mold.

The timeline: Police responded to a shooting inside VIDA Fitness, at 15th and P streets NW, just before 8am. Additional reports of shootings nearby followed.

  • Carroll said the shootings themselves likely unfolded in less than five minutes, though investigators are still reconstructing the timeline.
  • Police announced a sixth shooting victim — a woman with nonfatal injuries — on Friday morning, per the Washington Post.

The victims: Stuart was pronounced dead inside VIDA. Police say the gunman then returned to his apartment, where he fired at people below from an upper-level private balcony.

  • Two men and two women were hospitalized, one of whom suffered serious injuries.

The standoff: Lambert barricaded himself in his apartment, where he broke a gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire inside the apartment, per police. Flames were visible outside the building, but sprinklers helped contain the blaze.

  • Police recovered gasoline and other flammable materials.
  • Police negotiators heard a gunshot while speaking with Lambert by phone, after which he stopped responding. Officers forced entry and found him suffering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

The weapons: Investigators recovered a handgun, shotgun and rifle from Lambert's apartment. Carroll said the suspect used all three firearms, none of which were registered in D.C.

People stand behind police tape in Logan Circle early Thursday. Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
A U.S. Park Police helicopter flies above the scene. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
U.S. Marshal officers move position at the scene of the Logan Circle shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Residents cross a street as law enforcement responds to the shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Behind the scenes: Lambert had been fighting his condo association over alleged leaks and mold, per court records. He filed a lawsuit against the group in March 2025.

  • Months later, he told now-Washington Sun reporter Michael Brice-Saddler that he'd spent nearly $200,000 on legal and engineering fees.
  • In those interviews, Lambert said he knew Stuart's daily gym routine.

What we don't know: Police have not determined whether Lambert knew the five surviving victims or deliberately targeted them.

  • The precise timeline and extent of the suspected planning also remain under investigation.

Context: The shooting prompted a massive response from local and federal authorities, including MPD, D.C. Fire and EMS, U.S. Park Police, Metro Transit Police and other federal law enforcement agencies.

  • Asked whether the show of force was due to the shooting's proximity to the White House, roughly a mile away, Carroll said it was because police were responding to an active shooter. "The expectation is folks will go there to try to stop the loss of life," he said. Mayor Bowser confirmed the White House had been briefed.
  • President Trump has surged federal law enforcement in D.C. through his Safe and Beautiful Task Force. In a speech before the midterms last week, Trump declared D.C. "one of the safest cities in the country."
  • Asked about Trump's role in reducing crime during Thursday's morning briefing, Bowser pushed back: "I praise MPD for bringing down crime in the city, and I praise our prosecutors."

Editors note: This story has been updated to add details about a sixth shooting victim.

item.title: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
item.description:
The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad is in Washington Friday for talks with senior Trump administration officials about the war in Iran, according to three sources with knowledge of the matter.

Why it matters: The visit by Roman Gofman, one of Benjamin Netanyahu's closest confidants, comes as the Israeli prime minister is pressing President Trump to resume the war against Iran.

Driving the news: Gofman is meeting with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, the sources said. He is also expected to travel to Miami to meet White House envoy Steve Witkoff, one of the sources said.

  • Mossad, the CIA and the White House declined to comment.

State of play: Trump has so far rejected pressure from Netanyahu to return to combat. The two discussed the Iran war during a Nov. 5 call, per a U.S. official.

  • Instead, the president has sided with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE to continue the naval blockade and economic pressure campaign against Iran, while seeing if a deal is possible.
  • "I could end it immediately. At the request of the nations that I'm looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a little bit more civilly," Trump said on Thursday.
  • "Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while, because [Iran is] disintegrating. Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period."

The intrigue: Netanyahu has lost his majority in parliament after the Oct. 27 election in Israel.

  • His opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, has received a mandate to form a new government. It is unclear whether he'll be able to do so.
  • In the meantime, leaders of the Israeli opposition are concerned Netanyahu will try to launch an attack on Iran — or provoke Iran to attack Israel — in order to undermine Eisenkot's efforts, sources say. Netanyahu would be removed from power if Eisenkot succeeds.
  • On Thursday, Netanyahu met with Eisenkot for two hours and briefed him on the situation with Iran.
  • A source close to Eisenkot said he doesn't think the current situation demands immediate military action against Iran.

What they're saying: Eisenkot said in a statement Friday that he met with Netanyahu and his military secretary this week and "made it clear that I will not allow a lack of oversight" of the prime minister's actions during the government transition.

  • "For me, Israel's security takes precedence over every other consideration and must never be used as a means of political capital. This is also what I expect of all officeholders," Eisenkot said.

  • "I could end it immediately. At the request of the nations that I'm looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a little bit more civilly," Trump said on Thursday.
  • "Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while, because [Iran is] disintegrating. Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period."

The intrigue: Netanyahu has lost his majority in parliament after the Oct. 27 election in Israel.

  • His opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, has received a mandate to form a new government. It is unclear whether he'll be able to do so.
  • In the meantime, leaders of the Israeli opposition are concerned Netanyahu will try to launch an attack on Iran — or provoke Iran to attack Israel — in order to undermine Eisenkot's efforts, sources say. Netanyahu would be removed from power if Eisenkot succeeds.
  • On Thursday, Netanyahu met with Eisenkot for two hours and briefed him on the situation with Iran.
  • A source close to Eisenkot said he doesn't think the current situation demands immediate military action against Iran.

What they're saying: Eisenkot said in a statement Friday that he met with Netanyahu and his military secretary this week and "made it clear that I will not allow a lack of oversight" of the prime minister's actions during the government transition.

  • "For me, Israel's security takes precedence over every other consideration and must never be used as a means of political capital. This is also what I expect of all officeholders," Eisenkot said.

item.title: Bessent puts Megaspeed heat on Lutnick: "Commerce has the pen"
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Friday interview that while his department and others agreed on placing Megaspeed on a special list of companies that pose national security concerns, the Commerce Department "has the pen."

Why it matters: Bessent didn't deny reports of tension between him and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has come under scrutiny for his inaction over Megaspeed.

  • The Singapore tech company has been accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China, and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted he had an affair with an executive from the company.
  • The U.S. has identified the woman, Alice Huang, as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

Driving the news: "Treasury, War, USTR, and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC Friday morning.

  • "You ... have to ask them about their internal processes," he added.
  • The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Oil supplies bounce back, but prices are still high
item.description:
Oil markets are heading into an unusual period as the Iran conflict remains in dangerous limbo: The supply crunch is easing, but prices could stay stubbornly high.

Why it matters: While gasoline prices have dropped lately, don't expect pre-war levels anytime soon even as Middle East exports fitfully recover.

  • Getting oil out of the region is expensive, which filters down to consumers.
  • The threat of new attacks can keep oil costs higher, too, thanks to the risk premium embedded in prices.

The big picture: Traders are watching the state of potential diplomacy — and the possibility of a prolonged stalemate.

  • Oil prices jumped yesterday after President Trump said on his Truth Social that "we don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed."

Driving the news: Crude oil export levels bounce around, but have recently returned to pre-war levels at times, barrel-tracking firms and analysts say.

  • Yet shipping threats will "persist in 2027," and attacks spiked last month (see the chart above), per political risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft.
  • A new agreement on navigating the Strait of Hormuz would just be a piece of the puzzle — if it ever happens.

"The threat of a renewed wave of shipping attacks will remain high as long as the underlying confrontation over Iran's nuclear and missile programmes remains unresolved," the firm's analysis states.

Catch up quick: Tracking how much supply is returning is a moving target, and higher production from countries outside the Middle East — including the U.S. — matters too.

  • The oil market is "showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the International Energy Agency said this morning.
  • Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf region rose to 82% of pre-war levels last month, though recovery of refined product shipments is weaker, its monthly analysis states.

With supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict, IEA predicts the global market will return to a surplus this quarter.

Yes, but: Insurance and shipping costs are elevated, and that puts upward pressure on prices.

  • "Both Iran and the Houthis have demonstrated that they can severely restrict oil flows from the region using a range of attacks and tactics. This is something that will have to be priced in," Torbjorn Soltvedt, a senior Verisk analyst, tells me via email.
  • And there's no guarantee that higher tanker transit and increased shipments through pipelines that avoid the Strait of Hormuz won't be curtailed by fresh attacks.

Zoom in: Goldman Sachs estimates that the tanker market's "adaptation to Mideast shipping risks" accounts for most of the $20-per-barrel year-over-year increase in average costs for shipping oil.

  • These freight rates reflect vessel availability, insurance, fuel cost, logistics, travel distances and more.

What we're watching: It's unclear how much more oil can keep leaving the region in the near term, as intermittent attacks keep happening.

  • "The current recovery may be close to the limit of what the existing logistics system can sustain," HSBC's Kim Fustier said in a recent note.

The bottom line: "We would not equate [oil] exports with normality," Fustier writes.

  • She cited substantial volumes of well production that remain curtailed, lower refined product shipments, and "and the cost of sustaining exports."

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes
item.description:
The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence in hospitals and clinics is leading the nation's biggest physicians group to lobby for new legal protections if AI harms patients.

Why it matters: The use of increasingly sophisticated AI tools and recommendations is blurring the lines around negligence in health care, raising questions about whether doctors should be held responsible for decisions that rely on software.

  • There's added urgency as autonomous AI takes on more and more important medical tasks with less direct oversight.
  • The question is who's responsible when something goes wrong.

Driving the news: The American Medical Association this week called for federal and state legislation to protect physicians from liability when AI products injure patients, despite physicians using the tools as intended.

  • The group also is pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data.
  • Hospitals, health systems, insurers and health tech vendors should be responsible if the required use of specific AI products results in harmful errors, the AMA policy states.

Between the lines: The group's push comes as AI clinical tools are flooding the health system, unlocking new efficiencies but giving algorithms increasing power to make decisions like whether to order a diagnostic test or prescribe an expensive drug.

  • Legal and medical experts point to the possibility of triage errors, in which AI systems that process clinical histories, vital signs and imaging can misjudge the severity of a case without the attending doctor's knowledge.
  • The AMA also raises the possibility of an AI system making a plausible recommendation for treatment, but with incomplete laboratory results or an outdated diagnoses. In such cases, a physician may be unable to verify the inputs.
  • In cases where a patient is harmed, responsibility should fall on AI manufacturers and vendors — and possibly on health systems that require the AI systems' use — instead of through a medical malpractice claim against the physician, the AMA argues.

Context: There already have been lawsuits around algorithm-driven medical decisions, including a wrongful death case in Alabama involving a screening tool for heart abnormalities.

  • The software developer wasn't held liable because its licensing agreement left final medical decisions to doctors.

The big picture: Courts around the country are concluding that companies that design, train and deploy AI systems bear responsibility for what the systems do, said University of California, Davis professor Martin Hilbert, who studies the role of digital information and algorithms in society.

  • Accountability hinges on factors including who shares responsibility when multiple parties build an AI system, how to prove fault inside an opaque model, and what to do when damages surface only after the system is deployed.
  • "Different parties are responsible for different cases, and you can't just hold the end user responsible," he told Axios.
  • The AMA wants to address situations when use of an AI system is mandatory.

What we're watching: The Food and Drug Administration is weighing whether a new framework is needed for regulating AI-enabled medical devices.

  • But the agency oversees software that meets the definition of a medical device, not all of the AI in health care.
  • Hospitals generally support putting the onus on developers and vendors for monitoring the systems' performance, saying the "black box" nature of many systems can make it hard to identify flaws.
  • AdvaMed, the trade group representing device makers, is urging the FDA to continue using its current approaches for evaluating generative AI-enabled medical devices. It also wants the agency to avoid post-market monitoring that imposes added burdens regardless of a product's actual risk.

item.title: Democrats in power confront the social media trap
item.description:
Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries are both cautious, calm, compromise-minded leaders fantasizing about a serious, sensible Democratic-run Congress.

  • But social media is a temptress no party leader has tamed. The seduction of attention, likes and followers invariably proves too strong for the savviest, most self-promotional politicians to resist.

Why it matters: That's the lesson of the Internet Era of American Politics — the algorithms always win.

A few provocative members of Congress and online activists dominate the national conversation because they master the biggest social media platforms. That creates the impression that their views reflect a party, or a nation, when in reality they don't. And it shapes the party's image and agenda.

  • Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), vice chair of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus, told us: "Governing isn't about getting the most followers on X — it's about delivering actual results ... It's easy to scream and yell, and say no — it's much harder to figure out a way forward."

By the numbers:

  • Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed had 1.6 million Instagram followers as of Sept. 13. Today: 7.6 million and rising. One clip of him pulled an estimated 50 million-plus views across X, Instagram and TikTok.
  • Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, sits at 466,000 Instagram followers. A man who hasn't been sworn in has roughly 15x the leader's audience.
  • El-Sayed telegraphed this in July: "If you're Chuck Schumer, I'm pretty damn dangerous!" True.
  • Jeffries has nearly 1 million followers on Instagram. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has 9.8 million on her personal account alone.

Yes, President Trump remade the GOP. But social media sucked in countless others to try to copy him, pushing rhetoric or ideas few politicians would've touched in the past.

  • You see this in the rise of celebrity politicians who do little legislating but lots of instigating.
  • You see this in the explosion of not just Instagram, X and YouTube followers by politicians, but also in the many starting their own shows — unthinkable a decade ago. Several see themselves as content producers: California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas host podcasts while doing pretty important day jobs for big states. Trump started his own social media platform, Truth Social.
  • You see this in the daily media feeding frenzy when someone, somewhere goes viral because they lit up social media with a meme or menacing post.

The trap is springing before Democrats have even been sworn in:

  • Several incoming senators have publicly said they won't support Schumer as leader, calling for new blood and more fight. James Talarico of Texas has sidestepped the question for months.
  • Petitions to replace Schumer passed 100,000 signatures a day after launch. At Crooked Con, the post-election summit hosted in Washington last weekend by the parent company of "Pod Save America," the crowd booed and jeered his name all day.
  • The pressure worked: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who's thinking about a 2028 presidential run, announced Thursday night on MS NOW he'll challenge Schumer for majority leader.

Doug Sosnik, a top official in Bill Clinton's White House and closely followed analyst of Democratic politics, told us: "You would never know it from the internet or press coverage, but the fact is there are only 130,000 members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)."

  • "It has taken a while, but I think that Democrats have finally figured out that X/Twitter is not the real world," Sosnik added. "The best proof point of Democrats' 'getting this' was our success across the entire country."

What we're watching: The biggest siren song of the algorithm this next year will be impeaching Trump.

  • Schumer and Jeffries have tried to set a disciplined path focused on affordability, not impeachment.
  • Trump is prone to taking provocative actions that would juice talk of impeachment. A crowded presidential primary field will make the topic even more tempting — a massive distraction for the new Democratic majorities.

Reality check: Schumer only needs about 29 of his members to vote for him in a secret caucus vote. He'll likely win the room. But he's losing the feed, and the feed sets the narrative.

  • Among the senators-elect who say they won't vote for Schumer are Adam Hamilton of Kansas and Troy Jackson of Maine. Running against your own leader is now a red state play, too.

Accountability creep: In December, Jeffries waved off a Hegseth impeachment push. On Sunday, he said he was a "hard yes." (House Republicans tanked the effort on Tuesday.) Bernie Sanders, the incoming HELP chair, says Democrats may go after RFK Jr. next, alongside aggressive investigations into Trump's staff and family.

  • To be fair: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky forced the vote, and Jeffries tied it to an Iran war he says has driven up prices. But removal would take two-thirds of the Senate, which Democrats don't have. It was a Week 1 fight they couldn't finish.

The bitter truth is there's little market for moderation or sanity or heads-down, excruciating policymaking. This wasn't always true: Pre-internet, politics wasn't minute-by-minute combat and most media played by similar rules and stuck to daily rhythms.

  • So how can Schumer and Jeffries overcome this? You could argue no party is better positioned than Democrats to resist, or at least tame, the social media temptation.
  • The scale of the win gives them cover: at least 54 Senate seats to 44 and 255 House seats to 168, with some races still uncalled. That's Democrats' largest House majority since 2008, with a lead of nearly 14 points in the total House vote.

Democrats clearly won because voters are tired of Trump's ideas, rhetoric and tactics. They clearly won because they fielded very moderate candidates in very red states: flips in Kansas (which hadn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century), Iowa, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina. They clearly won because those candidates uniformly talked about the economy, the cost of living and things that matter to real people in real states.

  • Only the most delusional Democrats think they won because of the mass appeal of their party. They know they have a golden opportunity to reposition and rehabilitate the Democratic brand.

Flashback: The last time Democrats held a majority this big, after 2008, they lost 63 House seats two years later. Big majorities have more members, more factions and more people chasing virality.

  • Some top Democrats think the House and Senate should agree to focus on the one topic that unites them all, affordability, and allow room for debate but not distraction.

Schumer and Jeffries could state this emphatically every day.

  • They could also make plain that they plan to hold Trump and others accountable, but leave that to oversight committees and make it secondary to bringing down prices.

The bottom line: Democrats won the election on prices. They'll lose the majority on posts.

  • Axios' Alex Thompson contributed reporting.

Go deeper: Trump's imperial last act.
